10398-the-american-child:
Elizabeth McCracken published this study in 1913, with photographs by Alice Austin, to describe American childhood at home, at play, and at school. McCracken opens with a duchess copying her mother's home for her own children, a sign of her theme: home shapes the child. The tone is gentle, observant, and hopeful.

Chapters treat the child at home, at play, in the country, in school, in the library, and in church. Pictures show small girls, country boys, story hours, and hymn classes. Readers get a charming, period portrait of American children, useful for students of education and family life.
10454-tales-for-young-and-old:
This story collection, signed W. and R. C., gathers tales written when the older readers were younger and the young were infants. The preface presents them as interesting tales for all ages, mixing romance, moral lessons, and adventure. Many pieces first appeared in magazines or annuals of the early Victorian age.

The Bride's Journey opens the set in 1809, when French troops held Prussia and a French officer loved Adelaide Hext against her father's will. Other tales treat a home wreck, love at first sight, a pledge redeemed, and a locksmith of Philadelphia. Readers get a varied, old-fashioned storybook for family reading.
11039-a-woman-s-journey-round-the-world:
Ida Pfeiffer, a Viennese traveller, published this unabridged translation of her journey round the world, from Vienna to Brazil, Chile, Tahiti, China, India, Persia, and Asia Minor. Pfeiffer denies being a professed tourist, claiming only the gift of narrating simply what she saw and did. She insists that only a boundless desire for travel and knowledge could carry anyone through such hardships.

Chapters follow the voyage to Rio de Janeiro, excursions inland, the passage round Cape Horn, Valparaiso, Canton via Tahiti, Singapore, Ceylon, Madras, and Calcutta. Dancers in gold-embroidered muslin, musicians on drums and violins, and markets, temples, and ports fill the journal. Pfeiffer's plain account made her famous, and it remains a classic of women's travel writing.
11605-the-appetite-of-tyranny-including-:
G. K. Chesterton's wartime book argues the facts of the case first: England came into the European war for plain reasons, easy to state, before deeper claims are made. Chapters follow on the war on the word, the refusal of reciprocity, the appetite of tyranny, and the escape of folly.

Letters to an old Garibaldian extend the argument, with Prussia's princes shown as foes of democracy who yet present themselves as forerunners of the future. The book is a polemic of 1914-1915, written while the war was young, and it defends the Allied cause in blunt, paradoxical prose.
11715-the-eyes-of-the-world:
Harold Bell Wright's novel opens with a dedication to Benjamin H. Pearson, student, artist, and gentleman, met on the Pipe-Line Trail in the San Bernardinos. An epigraph from Wordsworth on nature and the sad, still music of humanity sets the tone.

Chapters follow an inheritance, a woman with a disfigured face, and the famous Conrad Lagrange. A girl who knows nothing of the world where the hero lives, except what Myra told her, offers music in a glade. The story moves between hills, orchards, and studios, and it asks how art, love, and a hidden past shape a life.
11717-the-palmy-days-of-nance-oldfield:
Edward Robins tells the palmy days of Nance Oldfield, the celebrated comedian, from tavern to theatre. Born in 1683 to Captain Oldfield's wife, under a star that danced, she rose to the stage in an age of Cibber, Congreve, and Wilks.

Chapters follow a belle of mettle, managerial wickedness, a dead hero, tragic paths, and Nance at home. The Kit-Cats, patriots who saved Britain, take their name, tradition says, from mutton pies. Portraits of Oldfield, Bracegirdle, Addison, and Steele illustrate the book. It is a stage history told as a lively life.
12026-poems-new-and-old:
John Freeman's Poems New and Old opens with press notices praising his landscapes. One critic writes that they have an individuality entitling him to his own place as a poet of nature. The New Statesman adds that appreciation of his lofty ardours, desolate landscapes, and strange, beautiful rhythms does not spring up instantly, but once arisen does not diminish.

Freeman's poems favor open country, solitude, and a music that is deliberately unlike easy lyric verse. The collection gathers new work with older poems, letting readers follow a poet whose reputation grew slowly, through attention to place and form rather than through fashion or display.
12283-the-soul-of-a-child:
Edwin Bjorkman published The Soul of a Child in 1922, a novel of boyhood in Stockholm. Bjorkman, a Swedish-American writer, sets the story on the rocky island that was once the whole city, where the Royal Palace faces the North River.

Keith, the hero, grows up near the Great Square, among schoolboys, summer holidays, and first friendships. A mid-book passage notes how other boys company can seem repulsive to a sensitive child, and how summer passes fast, with regrets at going home. Bjorkman traces a child inner life: fear, wonder, cruelty, and tenderness, without sentimentality. The novel is a quiet psychological study, praised for its honest portrait of growing up.
12360-the-top-of-the-world:
Ethel M. Dell's 1920 romance opens with Sylvia, a young woman left mistress of her own house, still faithful to a lover she has not seen for five years. Her old gardener urges her to marry, but she insists that only Guy Ranger will do. A prefatory poem sets the key: ascent by faith and love, not by wealth or fame.

Chapters titled The Punishment, The Parting, The Storm and The Sacrifice follow Sylvia through separation, temptation and hard choices. New suitors press their claims, old wounds reopen, and the long engagement is tested from both sides. Dell closes the arc, as the final chapter title promises, with faith and love rather than rank or money deciding who reaches the top.
12628-selections-from-the-prose-works-of:
William Savage Johnson's Riverside College Classics selection presents Matthew Arnold's prose with introduction and notes, published by Houghton Mifflin. Arnold, Victorian poet and critic, wrote essays on culture, education, religion and society that shaped English thought. Johnson, professor at the University of Kansas, frames them for college students.

Selections show Arnold's critical method: disinterestedness, sweetness and light, and the best that has been thought and said, applied to books, schools and churches. Footnotes, renumbered for this edition, follow their original page order. The volume serves as a classroom door into Arnold, clear, annotated and suited to first serious reading.
1292-the-way-of-the-world:
William Congreve's masterpiece follows Mirabell, a witty gentleman who schemes to marry Millamant, the wittiest woman in London. He must fend off her aunt, his own mistress, and a crew of fops and schemers. The play's dialogue is the finest of Restoration comedy.

Millamant's proviso scene, in which she sets the terms of marriage, remains famous, and the plot's intrigues resolve in a glittering finale. Congreve writes love as a game of wit played for high stakes. The play still crowns the Restoration stage, and it delights lovers of sharp talk.
13125-deer-godchild:
Deer Godchild, by Marguerite Bernard and Edith Serrell, published in 1919 for the Fatherless Children of France, tells a war charity in letters. A boy writes to Deer Miss Secretary, asking for a French orphan boy aged ten to twelve, and sends eighty-five cents, seventy for the first week and fifteen toward the next. His father at first objects, then agrees when the boy raises the money himself.

Letters run both ways, in broken spelling on both sides, full of jokes about school, dictionaries, and a Yankee woman with two tongues. A French child describes an American soldier, Teddy, in ground-colored uniform, hat tied like an old woman's bonnet, who teaches the verb avoir. The book is charming, funny, and humane, a child's-eye view of relief work after war.
13878-the-english-orphans-or-a-home-in-t:
Mrs. Mary J. Holmes published The English Orphans in 1877, a domestic novel of emigration and charity. English orphans cross to America and find work, hardship, and new homes. Chapters follow the emigrants, Chicopee, Billy Bender, and Ella Campbell. The poor-house, Sal Furbush, and the Lincolns mark the children's early trials.

Later chapters move to church, school, Mount Holyoke, and life in Boston. A new bonnet, winter at the poor-house, and a new home in Rice Corner give the tale its homely detail. Holmes writes with warm sentiment and a moral eye. A sick boy, George, tended by a girl smoothing his pillow, shows her touch. The novel suits readers of Victorian domestic fiction.
14021-lord-of-the-world:
Robert Hugh Benson's novel imagines a future Europe where faith has nearly vanished and a single world order rules. Percy Franklin, a Catholic priest, watches the rise of Julian Felsenburgh, a charismatic peacemaker whom crowds hail as a savior. London lies partly underground, its houses sunk below the Thames embankment, and old loyalties fade in the glare of the new age.

Persecution closes in as the story moves through three books: advent, encounter, and victory. Priests hide, families split, and believers face a choice between comfort and conscience. A mother's death, a rosary snapped in struggle, and a husband's quiet grief give the large theme a human scale. Benson wrote as a Catholic convert, and his warning still grips readers: a world that prizes unity above truth may crown a kindly tyrant and call it peace.
1415-doctor-marigold:
Told in the voice of a travelling Cheap Jack, this Christmas story follows Willum Marigold, a hawker who sells goods from a cart at fairs and markets. He tells of his trade, his patter, and his lonely life on the road, with the humour and plain speech of a man who lives by his wits.

The heart of the tale is Marigold's adoption of a deaf girl named Sophy. A bond grows between them as she learns to read his signs and share his work. It is a warm, sad, and funny story about found family, loss, and the small kindnesses of the road.
14176-the-dweller-on-the-threshold:
Robert Hichens's 1911 novel follows Evelyn Malling, known for psychical research and work for Professor Stepton, as he meets the Rev. Marcus Harding. Translated from Liverpool to a West End church, Harding draws London's largest Hospital Sunday collections, with music praised by connoisseurs of Elgar, Goss, Perosi, Bach, and Wesley. Success, however, hides a threshold Malling longs to cross.

Lady Sophia supplies the human pressure. Strung up and tormented by long-repressed feeling, she twists her gloves, drinks strong Academy tea, and longs to confide. Her husband rushes through modern life, she says, when one must keep rushing to reach any goal. Harding later begs Malling by letter not to speak to Professor Stepton of their Tankerton talk, citing obligations to others. Psychical inquiry, clerical reputation, and marital strain weave a subtle Edwardian mystery.
14515-the-nervous-child:
Hector Charles Cameron, physician to Guy's Hospital in London, wrote this 1919 study of nervous children, reprinted in 1930, for doctors and mothers. Cameron headed the children's department at Guy's.

Chapters cover appetite, sleep, enuresis, toys, and management in infancy and later childhood, with nursery observations at the core. Cameron warns against harsh Spartan methods for highly strung children, noting that a sobbing child often defeats the parent's resolve. The book is a humane early guide, dated in places but gentle in temper. Cameron urged parents to respect a child's solitude and fears.
14524-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
This 1885 volume of Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science, old series volume thirty-six, gathers a full year of the Philadelphia monthly's fiction, essays, and poetry. Some pages were missing from the manuscript and are marked.

Contents include a backwoods romance, birds of a Texas winter, a chapter of mystery, fishing on Elk River, and stories by Mary Agnes Tincker and others, plus monthly gossip and literature notes. The volume shows a general magazine serving many tastes at once. It is a rich sampler of American popular writing in the mid-1880s.
14599-light-on-the-path-and-through-the-:
This volume pairs two theosophical works written down by M. C., Light on the Path and Through the Gates of Gold, with notes and commentaries from Lucifer and The Path. The Light on the Path text reprints the 1888 edition.

Short rules for disciples open the first work: before eyes can see they must be incapable of tears, and before the voice can speak it must have lost the power to wound. The second work urges giving over taking and feeding the hungry over seeking manna. The book is a classic of modern esoteric teaching, brief, aphoristic, and earnest.
15802-with-botha-in-the-field:
A war memoir by Moore Ritchie, a lieutenant in His Majesty's Imperial Forces, issued by Longmans, Green and Company in 1915. Ritchie served with General Botha in the field, in the South African campaign of the Great War. Five diagrams and eighty-two pictures, mostly by the author, join the text. The book gives a soldier's view, not a staff history.

Marches, camps, and actions unfold through Ritchie's eyes, with Botha's leadership at the centre. Sketches catch men, horses, and country in quick lines. The tone stays modest and direct, praising comrades without boasting. The memoir serves readers who want the campaign as soldiers saw it: dust, orders, and endurance.
1605-the-crock-of-gold:
James Stephens's Irish fantasy opens with philosophers who can hear each other thinking all day, and a crock of gold hidden by leprechauns. Pan comes to the woods, a philosopher journeys in search of wisdom, and gods, policemen, and thin folk cross a tale that mixes folklore with philosophy and jokes.

Through six books, from the coming of Pan to the philosopher's return, Stephens writes of love, freedom, and the Irish countryside with lyrical wit. The book is strange, funny, and beautiful. It is a classic of the Irish literary revival, and a fantasy unlike any other.
16077-children-of-the-wild:
A book of animal stories by Charles G. D. Roberts, author of Kings in Exile, issued by the Macmillan Company in New York in 1922. Roberts, Canada's beloved nature writer, tells of wild babies and their first adventures. Each chapter follows a young creature learning the ways of the wild. The tone stays tender, vivid, and true to nature.

Little furry ones slide downhill, black imps haunt pine-top, and young Grumpy meets a one-eyed gander. Little Sword and the Inkmaker, a snowhouse baby, and a teddy bear's bee tree follow, with a baby and a bear, a little sly one, and Dagger Bill's water babies. The book delights young naturalists: wild children, brave and small, in a world made for wonder.
16150-miss-mcdonald:
Mrs. Mary J. Holmes's novel Miss McDonald builds its story from journals, diaries, and letters, a popular Victorian device. Contents move from extracts in the journals of Frances Thornton, Guy, and Daisy. An author's story, a divorce, and five years later follow. A letter from Daisy and scenes at Saratoga and in a sick-room close the book. The title character herself appears only in chapter ten, after the ground has been laid.

Love, marriage, separation, and reunion drive the plot, with Elmwood gardens and society watering places for scenery. Holmes, a best-selling domestic novelist, writes warm, moral tales of family feeling. Readers who enjoy old-fashioned stories of hearts tested and homes remade will find this a comfortable, engaging read.
16284-matthew-arnold:
George Saintsbury's Matthew Arnold, published by Blackwood in Edinburgh and London in 1902 in a third impression, belongs to a series on modern English writers. Companion volumes cover Stevenson, Ruskin, Tennyson, Huxley, Thackeray, George Eliot, Browning, Froude, and Dickens, each by a noted critic. Saintsbury, professor of rhetoric and English literature at Edinburgh, writes with authority and ease.

His preface notes Arnold disliked the idea of a regular biography, and that the only official sources for his life are the letters published by his family under G. W. E. Russell. The book therefore judges the poet and critic more than it narrates a life. Readers will find a classic early study of Arnold's poetry and prose.
16629-the-furnace-of-gold:
Philip Verrill Mighels wrote this 1909 western tale of gold claims, rivals, and love in the hills. Van, Beth, and Bostwick stand at the center, with partners, plots, a rescue, a battle, a shack moved by hand, and a night in the desert. Chapters run from a prince-or-bandit opening through dust storms, hard trails, and a timely rescue.

Mighels mixes mine work, song, tall tales, and fights with a love plot that keeps tightening. Beth's pluck and Van's grit meet Bostwick's schemes, and the gold claim itself tests each claim of honor. Fans of old westerns will find brisk scenes, plain heroes, and a story that moves fast from camp to court of public scorn and back.
16634-biltmore-oswald:
J. Thorne Smith Jr. of the U.S. Naval Reserve Force wrote this 1918 diary of a hapless recruit, first printed in The Broadside, a journal for the naval reserve. Stokes put it out in New York with thirty-one black-and-white drawings by Richard Dorgan. It follows Biltmore Oswald from enlistment through drill, shipmates, and petty officers.

Smith tells the tale in jokes and jibes, with a mock dedication to his buddies, his officers, and a dog he calls Mr. Fogerty. The humor is that of a green sailor meeting navy rules, hard beds, and loud mates. The book gives a light, first-hand laugh at wartime training, best read as a comic diary rather than a grave war record.
16745-matthew-arnold:
G. W. E. Russell wrote this short life of Matthew Arnold for the Literary Lives series, issued by Scribner's in New York in 1904 with pictures. It was offered to Arnold's children with love and memory. The series set Arnold beside Newman, Gaskell, Bunyan, Bronte, Goethe, and Hazlitt, each in one small volume.

Russell paints Arnold as wise, just, self-ruled, tender, and thankful, yet still reaching for something beyond. He tracks the poet and critic through school, verse, prose, and public work, and quotes the critics who shaped his fame. The life is a clear, warm first guide for readers new to Arnold, and a compact portrait for those who know his verse.
16861-the-wedge-of-gold:
C. C. Goodwin, editor of the Daily Tribune, wrote this 1893 mining tale, printed by the Tribune job office in Salt Lake City. Chapters move from the mineral kingdom and signs of ore into making money at four dollars a day. Bonanzas, dark ways, and ways miners are caught follow. Epsom Downs, Westminster Abbey, and Africa appear. A quartz mill shipped west closes the arc. Marriage bells close the book.

Goodwin mixes mine lore with travel, love, and stock deals, as a wedge of gold changes hands and fortunes. The tale shows the boom world of the West: hope, fraud, luck, and hard work side by side. Readers keen on mining history and old western tales will find a lively, plot-rich novel of the gold age.
16932-the-religious-life-of-the-zun-i-ch:
Mrs. Tilly E. Stevenson wrote this Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology study of the religious life of the Zuni child. Contents run from a brief account of Zuni myth, through birth customs, to involuntary and voluntary initiation into the Kokko. Plates show Zuni masks, Koyemshi figures, a sand altar in the Kiva of the North, and a Kiva of the East.

Stevenson records rites, masks, and kiva life as seen by an outside scholar of her day, with care for detail and order. The study gives a close, early account of Zuni childhood religion, valued by scholars of Native America. Modern readers should read it as a period ethnology, noting that Zuni voices and views have since reshaped the field.
17110-the-young-man-and-the-world:
Albert J. Beveridge's 1905 book speaks straight to young men facing work, home, and public life. Honesty is its first rule, and later chapters test that rule in college, the law, the pulpit, public speech, and the nation. Beveridge also writes of the old home, the new home, and facing the world again at fifty.

The tone is earnest and practical, full of short maxims and plain counsel about grit, study, and service. Some of its views belong firmly to its age, but its core plea still reads clear: do honest work, keep learning, and take part in civic life. It is a period advice book with vigor and a strong sense of duty.
17118-the-moving-picture-girls-under-the:
Laura Lee Hope's 1914 film adventure follows the Moving Picture Girls to Florida with their acting troupe. A fall overboard, a fire on board, and a broken ship start the trouble, and St. Augustine, motor races, and Lake Kissimmee fill the middle reels. Then the girls are lost in the wilds, where a palm hut and a long night test their nerve.

The book mixes early movie making with a survival tale: cameras, lights, and a stage boss share space with boats, trees, and strange attacks. Young readers get thrills without gore, plus a look at how films were shot on site. It is a brisk, sunny entry in a series built for fans of pluck and pictures.
17157-gulliver-s-travels-into-several-re:
Jonathan Swift's 1726 satire, edited here by Thomas M. Balliet with pictures and a map, sends Lemuel Gulliver to Lilliput, land of tiny folk, and Brobdingnag, land of giants. Shipwreck, capture, court life, and narrow escapes fill the early voyages, while later parts push the joke further into strange realms. The preface notes that children seized the book at once, even though Swift aimed at adults.

Under the adventure lies sharp satire on politics, pride, and human folly, told in plain, exact prose. Young readers love the scale jokes; older readers catch the sting. Few books have lasted so well in both roles, and this school edition keeps the tale clear for new readers of all ages.
1717-what-s-wrong-with-the-world:
Modern reform, Chesterton argues, goes wrong because it treats people as problems to be fixed rather than as members of families and homes. Chapters on the medical mistake, the new hypocrite, the fear of the past, and the enemies of property build toward a defence of the free family and of small ownership.

Chesterton writes against both big business and big government. His target is the expert who would remake the home in the image of the clinic or the factory. The essays are combative and witty, and they still provoke because they ask a plain question: if the home is broken, why do reformers keep prescribing cures that break it further.
17351-the-rivals-of-acadia-an-old-story-:
Issued in Boston in 1827 by Wells and Lilly, this early American novel bears no author's name on its title page. Its epigraph, taken from Shakespeare, warns what happens when two authorities are up and neither is supreme: confusion soon enters between them, and one is taken by the other. That warning frames a tale of rivalry in Acadia, the old French land of the New World.

Readers get a story of the New World written when the United States was barely fifty years old, in the formal prose of its day. The book's interest lies in its early date, its colonial subject, and its picture of divided rule. It suits readers of early American fiction and of the history of Acadia itself.
17521-everychild:
Louis Dodge published this allegorical story with Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1921, with pictures by Blanche Fisher Laite. The book presents itself as a story which the old may interpret to the young and which the young may interpret to the old. Its argument is plain: Everychild meets the giant Fear and sets out on a strange road.

On the way Everychild meets Aladdin of the wonderful lamp, is joined by Hansel and Grettel, and faces a dashing youth in the forest and a fight strangely ended. A frontispiece shows poor Cinderella, hinting at the fairy company kept. Readers get a gentle moral fantasy, where familiar tales lend their heroes to a child's lesson in courage.
17567-the-way-of-the-wild:
F. St. Mars wrote this book of wild animal stories, published in New York in 1919 by Frederick A. Stokes Company, with twelve pictures by Harry Rountree. The book appeared in England under the title Pinion and Paw. A frontispiece shows jaws, monstrous and wet, grabbing at a victim in enraged confusion, which sets the book's fierce tone.

Chapters follow Gulo the indomitable, Blackie and company, and life under the yellow flag. Nine points of the law, Pharaoh, and the cripple follow, with set a thief, the where is it, lawless little love, and the king's son ahead. Readers get animal tales told from the beasts' side, vivid and unsentimental.
18350-social-life-in-the-insect-world:
J. H. Fabre wrote this study of social life in the insect world, translated by Bernard Miall and published in London by T. Fisher Unwin, with fourteen illustrations. The first edition appeared in 1911, with many impressions through 1919. Fabre, the great French observer of insects, watches his subjects in the field rather than in the cabinet, and writes of them as living neighbors.

Chapters open with the fable of the cigale and the ant, then follow the cigale leaving its burrow, its song, and its eggs and hatching. The mantis follows, in chase, courtship, and nest, with plates showing a duel between females and a mantis devouring a cricket and her mate. Golden gardeners, field crickets, and Italian crickets close the set. Readers get natural history at its most vivid: insects hunting, singing, and rearing young, seen by a patient eye.
18442-fifty-famous-stories-retold:
James Baldwin retold fifty famous stories for young readers, published by the American Book Company in 1896. Baldwin chose tales that every schoolchild was once expected to know, and told them in short, plain chapters fit for reading aloud. The book served classrooms and homes as a first history in story form.

Contents open with King Alfred and the cakes, King Alfred and the beggar, and King Canute on the seashore. Later stories give Robin Hood, Bruce and the spider, and the Black Douglas. They also give the Miller of the Dee, Sir Philip Sidney, and Pocahontas. Washington and his hatchet, Grace Darling, William Tell, and Napoleon crossing the Alps close the set. Children get history as anecdote: kings, heroes, and famous deeds, each in a few pages.
18563-raw-gold:
Bertrand W. Sinclair wrote this western novel, published by G. W. Dillingham in New York in 1908, with illustrations by Clarence H. Rowe and copyrights in 1907 and 1908. Its chapters carry names like The Long Arm of the Law, Birds of Prey, Thirty Days in Irons, and Honor Among Thieves.

The story opens with a narrator looking back on golden years, sharp against the skyline of memory, and wishing he could live them again. Sinclair sets lawmen, outlaws, and riders against the western ranges, where a close call, a camp of the enemy, and a master-stroke of villainy drive the tale toward its end.
18581-adrift-in-new-york-tom-and-florenc:
Horatio Alger Jr. wrote this city adventure, published by A. L. Burt in New York in 1900. Alger, author of Mark Mason's Victory and Ben Bruce, sets his story among young people left to brave the world in New York, where honesty and pluck must answer for fortune.

The opening chapter, The Missing Heir, finds Florence Linden with her uncle. He says he is nearing the end and speaks of two great sorrows: his wife's death and the loss of his boy Harvey. Tom and Florence, adrift in the city, must make their way through that loss, and the novel follows their search for home, work, and kin.
18688-daisy-in-the-field:
Elizabeth Wetherell wrote this novel in 1868, here in a Ward Lock edition. It follows Daisy, now older, through scenes of war and waiting told in the first person. Chapters carry titles such as The First Smoke of the Battlefield, At the Rendezvous, On Foot, On Horseback, In the Fire, and The Wounded. A hospital, a truce, a flight, and old battlefields fill later pages.

The book opens at night by a fire, with Daisy too shaken to rest, turning to study while visions of a grey uniform mix with old kings and soldiers. Wetherell keeps the focus on patience, faith, and duty amid loss. The novel is a moving Civil War era tale for young readers.
18689-the-wide-wide-world:
Elizabeth Wetherell's 1850 novel, in this Tauchnitz author's edition of 1854, follows a young girl named Ellen through trials that test her temper and tenderness. The novel opens with Ellen beside her ailing mother, troubled by talk of her father's lawsuit, and traces her slow growth toward steadiness and self-rule.

A contemporary review quoted in the volume praised the book for building its heroine's character step by step on a religious base, rather than giving her sudden gifts of strength. Ellen stays gentle and tender through sorrow, yet grows firm enough to hold her place with quiet self-respect. The novel's fame rested on that slow, lifelike growth, which made many readers feel they were reading a true life.
18777-ruth-arnold:
L. Byerley's story of Ruth Arnold, the country cousin, published by the Religious Tract Society of London, opens in a summer holiday. Ruth, fourteen, walks home with a prize book, a new English grammar, feeling little pride in it and less pleasure.

She has sat at Miss Green's village school since she was six, saying rote lessons from elementary catechisms, and she doubts she has learned a single new thing all half-year. Chapters follow her letter, her decision, a journey, cousins at Stonegate, seaside pleasures, a picnic, school gossip, and an examination. The tale carries a country girl through town cousins, humiliation, and hard work toward home again.
19010-the-admirable-tinker-child-of-the-:
Edgar Jepson wrote this 1904 novel about Tinker, a lost boy found and trained by Sir Tancred. The boy, born Hildebrand Anne Beauleigh, vanished as an infant through a stepmother's scheme, and his father searched house agents and shops in vain. Tinker grows up sharp, brave, and loyal.

He rescues Elizabeth Kernaby, foils a baron and a money lender, and meddles in a stolen flying machine, among other scrapes. Each chapter gives him a fresh test of wit and pluck. Readers get a lively boys' tale of hidden birth, adventure, and a foundling who earns his name.
19308-pioneers-and-founders-or-recent-wo:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote this 1874 volume, Pioneers and Founders, on recent workers in the mission field, for Macmillan's Sunday Library. She gathers distinguished English and American missionaries of the last two centuries to show the character and growth of mission work, while setting Jesuit and Moravian missions aside as subjects apart. Reginald Heber fronts the book.

Yonge describes island missions torn by quarrels between London missionaries and rivals, while whalers and sandalwood traders bring vice and violence, and islanders are kidnapped for labour in Australasian settlements. Schools and chapels still rise, chiefs accept Christian codes, and cannibalism ends. Readers get a Victorian mission history, earnest and colonial in outlook.
19453-the-shield:
Maxim Gorky, Leonid Andreyev, and Fyodor Sologub edited this volume in defense of the Jews of Russia, translated from Russian and issued in New York in the late nineteen teens. William English Walling supplies a foreword, and Russian writers of many views add essays, stories, and appeals.

The core case is that Jews served Russia's trade, crafts, and industry, and that hatred of them harmed Russia itself. More than a plea for one people, the book claims to reveal the Russian mind at a moment of crisis. It is a landmark of wartime protest writing, plain in its moral aim.
20025-pirate-gold:
F. J. Stimson published Pirate Gold in 1895, a novel built around money held by an old bank. The bank had taken a national charter in 1863, during the Civil War. Yet some gold sat on no account and in no reserve. That odd gap sits at the heart of the tale.

Stimson writes about bankers, clerks, and the paper money of a new national system. Greenbacks, specie, and old habits of trade all shape the plot. Readers get a story of finance told from inside the counting room, not from a textbook.
20417-the-outline-of-science-vol-1-of-4-:
The Outline of Science, first published in 1922, set out to explain modern science to general readers. This is the first of four volumes. Its makers called the plain reader the man in the street, and wrote for him in simple, direct language.

The book offers what its preface calls a bunch of keys for locked doors. Behind those doors lie the treasures of knowledge about the heavens, the earth, and living things. Diagrams and clear chapters break hard ideas into steps. The set became a well-known doorway into science for readers with no training.
20453-the-christmas-child:
The Christmas Child is a Christmas story set on a poor farm by the sea. The land is hard to work. In every field, rocks pierce through the thin soil and stand out, grey and sharp, amid the grass and the ripening corn.

Salt-laden winds beat the farm, and money is scarce. Against that hard setting, the tale sets the season's hope and the coming of a child. Stories of this kind were written to be read aloud at Christmas. They found their warmth in simple homes, where kindness had to cover what wealth could not.
20817-the-mother-and-her-child:
No calling stands higher, says The Mother and Her Child, than that of a healthy mother. Business wives, farm wives, and wives of wealth all share one deep instinct. That claim frames a guide to pregnancy, birth, and infant care.

Doctors Lena and William Sadler wrote plain health books for American homes. This one treats feeding, illness, growth, and daily care in clear terms. It aimed to cut infant deaths with sound, calm advice. Readers today can see both the good sense and the firm moral tone that marked home health guides of the early twentieth century.
20834-ruth-fielding-at-the-war-front-or-:
No passer-by could miss Ruth Fielding, with her cheerful eye and humorous lip. At the War Front sends Ruth to France in 1918 to hunt a lost soldier. Alice B. Emerson's heroine had grown from school tales to war service by this volume.

Ruth works near the lines, facing peril with pluck and good sense. The lost soldier hunt gives the plot its pull and its heart. Girls' series books joined the war effort in their own way, with heroines who served bravely. This entry shows Ruth at her most grown-up, in khaki days far from her schoolgirl start.
21627-gambler-s-world:
Retief of the Corps Diplomatique checks his vermilion cutaway in Keith Laumer's Gambler's World, from Worlds of If in 1961. Four sets of lapels mark his rank as First Secretary and Consul. Magnan calls him to the ambassador's briefing before the Potentate enters.

On Petreac, the Nenni hold authority, and their traditions must be observed. Retief's mocking air, Magnan warns, has already delayed his rise. The trade talks have been scripted for two months, yet Retief treats them as a gamble. Laumer's Retief tales mix diplomacy, poker faces, and sly humour in a brisk space-age key.
21730-erling-the-bold:
Vikings row out from a Norwegian fiord on a bright summer morning at the start of this Ballantyne tale of old Norway. Two boats head for the same rocky islet but keep apart, their crews wary of each other. The men wear ring mail and steel headpieces, armed as men had to be in those days.

Erling, the bold hero of the title, leads the story through feuds, voyages, and fights. Ballantyne loved the northern seas, and he fills the tale with ships, storms, and the hard code of the Norsemen. It is his take on the saga world: proud men, sharp swords, and honor held dearer than life itself.
22093-the-sagas-of-olaf-tryggvason-and-o:
Two Norse kings share this volume of sagas in English dress. Olaf Tryggvason forced Norway toward Christianity at the end of the tenth century. Harald the Tyrant, better known as Harald Hardrada, was the last great Viking king. He fell at Stamford Bridge in 1066, weeks before Hastings changed England for good.

The Olaf chapters show a queen hiding by night as winter closes in. Enemies hunt her party through a frightened countryside. Battles, conversions, and sudden deaths fill both sagas, told in the spare saga style. These translations brought the kings' lives from the Icelandic histories to English readers who knew Norway mainly through its Vikings.
22593-the-shadow-world:
Hamlin Garland wrote The Shadow World, a 1908 book about psychical research and the puzzle of hypnotism and spirit claims. Garland, a well-known American novelist of farm life, turned late in his career to the study of mediums and mental phenomena. Here he reports talks and sittings with a skeptical, watchful eye.

In the sample scene, a man named Miller answers slowly. He believes in Vienna, though he has never seen it. Yet he doubts a Vienna doctor who claims he can hypnotize a patient into smiling through an amputation. That blend of faith and doubt runs through the book. Garland tests wonders against plain reason, case by case. Readers curious about the era's seance culture get a thoughtful, firsthand tour.
22938-the-camp-fire-girls-in-the-outside:
Margaret Vandercook sends her heroines beyond camp in The Camp Fire Girls in the Outside World, published in 1914. One scene turns on small, telling action. Entering the drawing room, a girl places candles on the mantelpiece. Her breath clouds faintly in the cold room. Her gown, mist-gray and clinging, suits the wintry light around her.

The Camp Fire Girls series followed its troop from woods and campfires into school, work, and the wider world promised by the title. Vandercook wrote for the new century's organized girlhood, mixing adventure with ideals of service and self-reliance. This volume's outside world tests camp lessons against city life. Period charm and period assumptions travel together through every chapter.
22974-the-city-bride-1696-or-the-merry-c:
Verse fireworks open The City Bride, a comedy of 1696 subtitled The Merry Cuckold. Pray aloud to this audience, one wit warns, and you merely oblige them, canonizing a crowd with no religion at all. Praying to such saints, he adds, can hardly count as superstition. The rhymes snap like a fan.

Restoration comedy lived on cuckolds, citizens, and sharp wives, and a city bride was its favorite engine. Money marries up, wit marries down, and everyone schemes in couplets and quick prose. Plays of this date mixed song, dance, and insult in roughly equal shares. The text preserves a minor but lively specimen, useful to anyone tracing how London laughed at marriage and trade at the century's end.
23022-red-rose-and-tiger-lily-or-in-a-wi:
Mrs. L. T. Meade introduces Hester Thornton in Red Rose and Tiger Lily, subtitled In a Wider World. Hester leaves the Grange drawing room and walks a short stretch of its wide gravel sweep, listening hard. She was about seventeen, slender for her age, with dark eyes, strongly marked brows, and abundant lighter brown hair coiled round her well-shaped head.

Meade wrote dozens of girls' novels, and Hester's step into a wider world follows her proven path. School friendships widen into society, with its tests of loyalty and love. The Grange's gravel sweep is the threshold. Beyond it wait the wider world's pleasures and snares. The book offers period girls' fiction at full polish, earnest, romantic, and sure of its moral ground.
23063-the-lost-child:
Sunlight does magic in The Lost Child, a tale dated 1894. Overnight sleet powdered every bare branch along the boulevard Malesherbes, outside the Godefroy mansion. The great magician sun, the narrator says, amused himself by turning those branches into great bouquets of red coral.

Paris sparkles first, then darkens, as a child goes missing inside the fine neighborhood. The contrast carries the story, beauty on the street, fear in the house. Tales of lost children were a period staple because they joined every reader's worst worry to a city's glitter. This one dresses the worry in lovely prose, and its boulevard opening remains its most quoted passage.
23140-the-death-shot-a-story-retold:
A modern editor confesses in The Death Shot, a story retold. The editor likes to think Reid would approve. Their version, he claims flatly, beats the published book, though some errors survive in it anyway. It makes a very nice audiobook, he adds, taking almost fifteen hours to read. He has heard it twice, and enjoyed it thoroughly.

That odd frame belongs to a retold version of Mayne Reid's frontier romance of love, jealousy, and a deadly rifle shot on the prairie. The retelling's presence raises its own questions about texts and tinkering, which the preface answers with disarming cheer. Readers get a long western of the old school, plus a small modern mystery about who improved it and why.
23150-the-albert-gate-mystery-being-furt:
Reginald Brett rests between cases in The Albert Gate Mystery, published in 1904. Work has been scarce since the celebrated case of Lady Delia Lyle's vanishing and death. Only a hard worker, Brett reflects, truly enjoys healthy idleness. A letter arrives as he dresses, inviting him to a quiet country shoot.

Louis Tracy's gentleman detective, Brett, takes further adventures here, as the subtitle promises, and a country shoot is exactly where mysteries find such men. Albert Gate, in Knightsbridge, gives the case its London address and its social shine. Tracy wrote brisk, romantic detection for readers who liked their sleuths well dressed and well connected. Idleness ends, as it must, with the first shot out of place.
23334-natural-law-in-the-spiritual-world:
Henry Drummond, a Scottish writer on science and faith, argued in this book that the same laws seen in nature also rule the life of the soul. Chapters take up birth, growth, death, decay, surroundings, and the pull of habit, each first laid out as a law of living things.

Drummond then maps each law onto conduct and belief: how a life grows or withers, how it feeds off others like a parasite, and how it fits its true type. The prose stays clear and earnest, aimed at readers torn between science and religion. Its fame rests on that bold bridge, which made old doctrines sound fresh by stating them in the terms of the natural world.
23335-unwise-child:
Randall Garrett wrote this science fiction novel, brought out by a New York house in the early nineteen sixties. Its center is a robot brain, an intelligent mind built by roboticists who must teach it step by step, lest too many shocks at once make it collapse or refuse to learn.

A character named Leda explains the care needed, likening the mind to lead that must recover between blows. Garrett's novel asks what it means to raise a machine mind as one would raise a child, with patience, limits, and hope. Snookums, the robot mind, is strictly logical yet unstable, since it works in a more than logical universe.
23448-heart-of-gold:
Ruth Alberta Brown wrote this girls' book, copyrighted in nineteen fifteen, about a girl who takes a dare and learns its cost. Peace, the heroine, joins a scrap book brigade, meets Gussie's new play, hears the lilac lady's message, and faces the bitter truth behind a dare gone wrong.

Parsonage twins, an endless chain of kindness, and school and home scenes fill the chapters, with a frontispiece cry of peace, come down, you will fall. Brown writes with warmth for young readers, mixing fun, fright, and moral growth in plain scenes. Girls who like school stories with heart will enjoy Peace's path from daring to care, and the friends who help her set things right.
23494-notable-voyagers-from-columbus-to-:
W. H. G. Kingston and Henry Frith wrote this long, profusely pictured history of notable voyagers, from Columbus to Nordenskiold, covering great sea journeys from the earliest days to the end of the nineteenth century. More than one hundred pictures, some small tail pieces and most full scenes, fill the book.

Columbus leads, and the search for the North West Passage, the true story of Alexander Selkirk, the real Robinson Crusoe, and a host of adventurers follow in turn. The prose keeps a middle path, neither too terse nor too full, holding interest while giving real detail of ships, coasts, and crews. Young readers and armchair travellers will enjoy a grand tour of exploration, told with zest and a love of the sea.
265-the-life-and-death-of-cormac-the-ska:
Cormac the Skald, poet and champion of tenth-century Norway and Iceland, loves and fights through a saga life. The Life and Death of Cormac, translated by W. G. Collingwood and J. Stefansson in 1901, draws on an Icelandic text from about 1250 to 1300. King Harald Fairhair rules when the tale begins.

Cormac's forefathers, sea-roving, and battles fill the opening chapters. His verse, his feuds, and his doomed love for Steingerda drive the rest. The saga mixes poetry, violence, and dry humor. It gives readers a vivid window on Viking-age Iceland.
2667-the-vicar-of-wakefield:
Oliver Goldsmith wrote this tale as if by the vicar himself, and it follows Dr. Primrose, a good clergyman whose family falls from comfort into trouble. The vicar's children, his wife, and his hopes for them carry the story through twenty nine chapters of mishap and recovery.

Fortune, rogues, and a lost daughter test the family's faith, while Goldsmith keeps his tone gentle and comic. The novel charms as a story of virtue rewarded, told with irony and warmth. It has stayed in print ever since as a beloved English classic, short, humane, and full of heart.
2807-to-have-and-to-hold:
Mary Johnston wrote this romance of colonial Virginia, dedicating it to the memory of her mother. The hero throws ambs ace, meets Master Jeremy Sparrow, marries in haste, and repents at leisure, in chapters that announce their own plots.

A woman has her way, the party goes to Jamestown, and prepares to fight, in a story of love, adventure, and the early colony. Johnston writes with dash and historical color. The novel became a bestseller, and it remains a rousing tale of Virginia's founding days. Jamestown's stockade frames a love story and a war.
2830-reginald:
Saki, the pen name of H. H. Munro, introduced Reginald in sketches first printed in the Westminster Gazette and collected in 1904. Reginald pronounces on Christmas presents, the Academy, the theatre, worries, house parties, and the Carlton, always with a cool and insolent wit. Each sketch lets its hero demolish some polite convention in a few lines of dialogue.

The comedy sharpens when Reginald meets would-be improvers, such as a lady who tempts him toward the strenuous life with strawberries and cream and a choir outing. He takes up each new cause with dangerous enthusiasm and drops it just as fast. The book endures as the purest form of Saki's humor, elegant, heartless, and quotable.
2841-the-ivory-child:
H. Rider Haggard returns to Allan Quatermain in The Ivory Child, opening with the hunter giving a shooting lesson and making a bet. Miss Holmes, a gold mine of doubtful value, and Lord Ragnall's story pull Quatermain from England toward Africa. There Harut and Marut, a plot, and a desert meeting lead to capture, curses, and a chase. Hans steals keys, a sanctuary oath is sworn, and an embassy tests the hero's nerve.

The adventure mixes treasure hunting with Haggard's familiar world of hidden kingdoms and ancient powers, including the ivory child Jana. Quatermain narrates with dry humor even when the danger sharpens. The book suits readers who want a full Quatermain quest, with rifles, desert marches, and a lost ruler at its heart.
2895-following-the-equator-a-journey-aro:
Mark Twain wrote Following the Equator as the record of a lecture tour around the world, inscribed to his young friend Harry Rogers. Twain warns the boy to form himself more closely on the author's model, then undercuts the advice with Pudd'nhead maxims gathered from observation rather than practice. The contents carry the party across America to Vancouver and aboard the steamer Warrimo.

Twain's humor ranges from shipboard captains and gritty pursers to a Mark Twain Club at Corrigan Castle in Ireland, founded in his honor twenty years before. The book mixes travel notes with jokes about empire, missionaries, and human nature. It remains the fullest account of Twain as a world traveler, funny even when his targets are serious.
2991-sir-francis-drake-s-famous-voyage-r:
Francis Pretty, one of Drake's gentlemen at arms, narrated Sir Francis Drake's Famous Voyage Round the World, prepared from a 1910 edition. The voyage began on November 15, 1577, when Drake sailed from Plymouth with five ships and barks and 164 gentlemen and sailors, giving out a pretended voyage for Alexandria. Contrary winds forced him into Falmouth Haven the next morning. The narrative follows the fleet into the South Sea and around the globe.

Raids yield eight hundredweight of silver in bags and fifty-seven wedges of silver, each about twenty pounds and shaped like a brickbat, taken at Arica. The barks stood empty, their crews gone ashore trusting no strangers. Pretty's account remains a vivid primary source for Drake's circumnavigation.
3076-ten-days-that-shook-the-world:
John Reed wrote Ten Days That Shook the World as an eyewitness history of the Russian October Revolution. Reed, an American journalist in Petrograd, follows the fall of the Provisional Government and the committee for salvation. The revolutionary front, counter-revolution, and victory fill ten chapters, with footnotes, appendices, and seventeen graphic figures. His preface and notes explain the book's method. Reed's scenes bring the revolution to life, including a meeting with Krylenko, whose fixed grin of extreme fatigue breaks when a friend recalls their shared prison days.

The book's sympathy for the Bolsheviks is open, and its reporting remains vivid. It stands as the classic firsthand account of October 1917 in English.
3103-a-little-journey-in-the-world:
Warner first meant to call this novel A Dead Soul, then dropped the title because Gogol's Dead Souls covered different ground. Gogol exposed a fraud built on selling the names of dead serfs with land; Warner instead traces how familiar social pressures wear down a woman's soul. In a note dated Hartford, 11 August 1899, he admits he could not force Margaret's story to its bitter, logical end.

The novel opens among friends talking about the lack of variety in American life, then follows its heroine through the world of wealth, fashion, and reputation. Its interest lies less in plot twists than in moral drift: small choices, made under steady social pressure, that slowly change a character from within.
3189-sketches-new-and-old:
Mark Twain gathers his early sketches in this volume, old favorites beside new pieces. The jumping frog leads the familiar names, with the stories of the bad little boy and the good little boy close by. Journalism in Tennessee, political economy, and my watch show Twain learning his trade in public. Answers to correspondents and the office bore sharpen his comic voice.

Later sketches, like the McWilliamses and their membranous croup, prove the mature humorist at work. The book traces Twain from newspaper jester to American classic in one set of short pieces. New readers get a quick tour of his range; old readers get the jokes that made his name, in the order he chose to keep them.
3267-old-love-stories-retold:
Richard Le Gallienne retells old love stories in this volume, but the hosted text holds only one of them. The file's own note says so plainly: at present we have only this one chapter, the story of Heinrich Heine and his Mathilda. The German poet and the wife of his later years are the whole of what the reader gets here.

That single retelling still shows Le Gallienne's method: an old love taken up gently and told anew for modern readers. Heine, exiled and ill, and Mathilda, his devoted companion, make a tender subject. Readers should know the limit before they open it: one complete love story, not the full shelf the title promises.
3317-now-it-can-be-told:
Philip Gibbs, the great war correspondent, writes what wartime censorship hid in this memoir. His preface states the purpose: aspects of the war the world must know and remember, not only as a memorial of men, but as a record of truth. The contents run from observers and commanders and the school of courage to the nature of a battle and a winter of discontent.

The heart of a city, psychology on the Somme, and the fields of Armageddon follow, closing with for what men died. Gibbs writes with a reporter's eye and a mourner's temper. The generals, the trenches, and the questions that outlived the guns: Gibbs watched them daily, and wrote them down.
3809-the-master-of-the-world:
Jules Verne brings back Robur the Conqueror in this sequel, now master of a machine that runs on land, swims, dives, and flies. A federal police inspector at Washington takes charge of the case when strange doings shake the Great Eyrie in the mountains and a new engine appears on roads, shores, and skies. Witnesses agree on speed, silence, and the lack of steam or smell, whether the marvel shows as one machine or three.

Newspapers demand that the government buy the invention at any price, lest European powers seize it first. The chase leads to the Terror itself, to Niagara, and to the Eagle's Nest, where Robur faces the law. Readers who like Verne's inventor tales will find a brisk thriller, with a villain who claims the whole world as his workshop.
4010-marmion-a-tale-of-flodden-field:
Sir Walter Scott's long narrative poem tells of Lord Marmion, a bold knight whose plots and pride carry him toward the Battle of Flodden Field. Monks, nuns, and border lords cross his path, and a grim Vault of Penitence holds those who died in mortal sin.

Scott mixes romance, history, and border legend, with Scotland's 1513 defeat looming over the tale. The verse moves between castle halls, convent cells, and the field itself, where Marmion's fate is sealed. Readers who enjoy historical romance in verse will find a stirring, old-fashioned epic of love, treachery, and war on the Anglo-Scottish border.
4019-the-lure-of-the-labrador-wild:
Dillon Wallace tells the true story of Leonidas Hubbard Junior's 1903 trip into the wild interior of Labrador, a journey that ended in hardship and death. Wallace, who traveled with Hubbard, writes from camp notes and memory of lakes, trails, and failing food.

The party pushes beyond the trappers' zone into country no white man seemed to have seen, picking camp sites near lake outlets and losing the trail again and again. Hunger, cold, and hard choices shape the march. The book stands as a plain, moving record of exploration gone wrong, and of friendship tested by the North.
4034-the-untilled-field:
George Moore's stories of Ireland center on country people, priests, and exiles whose lives are shaped by land, faith, and want. A sampled tale, The Exile, opens at fair time, as Pat Phelan readies bullocks and pigs for sale while his sons divide the farm work.

Moore writes with a plain, unsparing eye for Irish villages, where a bargain, a churning, or a parting can carry a whole life. The untilled field of the title stands for talent and land left unused under old rule. Readers who like quiet, realist stories will find a book of lasting force and sad beauty.
4301-the-nether-world:
George Gissing set this novel in the poorest quarters of London, among families for whom life is a daily thralldom. The contents move from a thrall of thralls and a friend in request to Clara and Jane, Mrs. Byass's lodgings, Pennyloaf Candy, and a soup kitchen. Later chapters bring phantoms, a barren shore, and woman and actress.

The nether world here is not hell but the lower depths of the city, where work is scarce and hope is scarcer. Gissing follows several households through disappointment, illness, and rare sunlight in dreary places. It is one of his darkest London books, and one of the most praised for its force.
4593-friends-and-neighbors-or-two-ways-o:
T. S. Arthur edited Friends and Neighbours, or Two Ways of Living in the World, published at Philadelphia in 1856, gathering material culled from the highways and byways of literature. His preface quotes fitting sentiments whose authorship he cannot give, and he says they express his own mind clearly. If we looked at the subjects around us in their true light, he argues, we would see beauty where deformity appears, and hear harmony where we hear only discord.

The volume's lesson is steady conduct in a vexed world: keep a calm eye and a steady hand, trim sail and manage helm, avoid quicksands, and weather storms that threaten shipwreck. We are members of one great family, travelling the same road toward the same goal, breathing the same air. Readers get a set of short, improving pieces about neighbourliness, patience, and the two ways a life can be lived among others.
4604-the-clique-of-gold:
Emile Gaboriau opens The Clique of Gold in Paris, at No. 23 in Grange Street. It is a house better kept than any in its street. Brass on the door shines like a mirror, stone floors are polished, and stair woodwork is varnished. Notices in the hall beg tenants to respect the property of others, to clean their feet, not to spit on the stairs, and to keep dogs out of the house.

Yet this admirably kept house enjoys a sorry reputation in the neighbourhood, worse in talk, if not in fact, than No. 21 or No. 25. Gaboriau, a founder of the French detective novel, uses the gap between polish and repute to open a mystery of money, family, and crime. Readers get a classic Paris intrigue, where a neat front hides a tangled past, and where detection begins with watching a house and its people closely.
4628-the-iron-rule-or-tyranny-in-the-hou:
T. S. Arthur published The Iron Rule, or Tyranny in the Household, at Philadelphia in 1853, complete in one volume. Andrew Howland belongs to a stern school of moralists who allow others no straying from the proper path. From babyhood his children are pressed into outward uniformity, and any step off the set line brings certain punishment.

Even a harsh, unreasonable parent, Arthur notes, still draws a child's natural love. The child gazes upward in helpless reliance, with affection threading through fear and respect like bright strands in dark cloth. From that household grows a tale of tyranny, obedience, and its costs. Readers get a stern Victorian domestic novel about authority at home, and about what rigid rule does to children who must live under it.
4654-the-daemon-of-the-world:
Percy Bysshe Shelley called The Daemon of the World a fragment, in two parts, opening with a Latin passage from Lucan on ages heaped into one mass pressing on a wretched breast. Part one asks how wonderful Death is, and his brother Sleep. One is pale as the wan, horned moon, with lips of lurid blue. The other glows like vital morning throned on ocean's wave. Both, Shelley says, are passing strange and wonderful.

Yet an iron-sceptred skeleton reigns in tainted sepulchres, with hell dogs beneath his throne. The poem asks whether the divinest form, whose azure veins steal like dark streams across snow, must decay into loathsomeness and ruin. Shelley turns death into a moral question, not a mere horror. Readers get a short, intense Shelley fragment, best read aloud, where beauty, decay, and the hope beyond death contend in high Romantic verse.
4687-saturday-s-child:
Kathleen Norris published Saturday's Child as volume four of her works. An old rhyme stands at its head. Friday's child is loving and giving, the rhyme says, but Saturday's child must work for her living. Norris dedicates the book to C. G. N., in a poem saying no living word of hers could exist without the echo of the dedicatee's own. Under that hand, as under hers, the book has grown.

Happy days, happy talks, hoping, and fears made this story of a happy life, Norris says. She offers her portion in dear memory of words of praise and four busy years, signing as wife. Part one is called Poverty, and chapter one opens in a dingy, narrow office on the mezzanine floor of a great wholesale drug house in San Francisco. Readers get a popular novel of a working girl, poverty, and perseverance, in Norris's warm style.
502-desert-gold:
Zane Grey sets this border romance in the Arizona desert, where prospector Cameron haunts Forlorn River. A woman's face from his past in Peoria drives him to solitude, gold hunting, and long nights by dying fires. Mercedes Castaneda, a Yaqui, white horses, and a bandit named Rojas soon pull him into flight and fight.

Grey writes the desert in vivid color, from cactus and lava to the crater of hell. Love, guilt, and a lost son shape the plot toward gold and grace. The novel stands as a classic western romance, where harsh land tests men and women alike.
5191-the-case-of-summerfield:
William Henry Rhodes's Case of Summerfield, introduced by Geraldine Bonner, belongs to the California short-story tradition that followed Bret Harte. Bonner's introduction recalls Harte's Luck of Roaring Camp and the line of successors who wrote realistic, romantic, tragic, humorous. Weird tales of the West follow, rescuing good work that had been lost in newspaper columns.

The volume presents Rhodes's stories as examples of that neglected California writing. Readers interested in the literature of the Gold Rush and its aftermath will find here short fiction rooted in mining camps, frontier towns. The mixed fortunes of the people who lived there fill the stories.
5702-masters-of-the-guild:
L Lamprey's Masters of the Guild, published in New York in 1920, tells stories of medieval craftsmen, apprentices, and the guilds that shaped their work. Its contents include Peirol of the Pigeons, A Tournament in the Clouds, The Puppet Players, and further tales of jesters, abbots, and lessons learned at the bench. Illustrations by Florence Choate and Elizabeth Curtis accompany the text.

Each tale shows a craft as a way of life, with rules, masters, pride, and the slow earning of skill. Young readers meet pigeons, puppets, tournaments, and workshops, and they learn how medieval towns honored honest work. The book suits children curious about the Middle Ages, and adults who enjoy clear, old-fashioned stories about making things well.
5896-her-weight-in-gold:
McCutcheon's Her Weight in Gold opens with the three Van Winkles, turned out of house and home by their father. Mr Van Winkle acts not from lack of love for his sons. He acts because he loves them well. The chapter introduces Courtney Van Winkle, nicknamed Corky by his irrepressible brothers, besides the twins, Jefferson and another brother. From that expulsion, a comedy of fortune and affection begins.

Readers follow young men forced to make their way, with a heroine whose worth gives the title its meaning. McCutcheon writes with polished, lighthearted ease, favoring witty dialogue and romantic complication over stern realism. The book suits fans of early twentieth-century popular romance, and readers who enjoy stories where love proves heavier than gold.
6007-the-two-sides-of-the-shield:
Charlotte M. Yonge revives figures from her early tale Scenes and Characters, answering youthful letters that begged for news of schoolroom favorites. She cites Shakespeare's revival of Falstaff at Queen Elizabeth's behest, while calling that great precedent a poor excuse for her own small return to old characters.

Yonge aims to make the new story stand alone for readers who never met Lady Merrifield and her brothers and sisters. Her preface notes that the household once ruled by duty may now be ruled by love, with confusion dire among the younger boys. The novel follows old friends into new trials and affections.
6317-sailing-alone-around-the-world:
Captain Joshua Slocum, of blue nose ancestry and Yankee ways, tells how he lost the Aquidneck, came home from Brazil in the canoe Liberdade, and received the gift of a ship. He rebuilt the Spray, solved puzzles of finance and calking, and launched her, then failed as a fisherman and projected a voyage round the world alone. From Boston to Gloucester he fitted out, with half a dory for a boat.

The Spray runs to Nova Scotia, meets fog off Sable Island, and finds the open sea, where the man in the moon takes an interest and loneliness first bites. A bottle of wine from a Spaniard, words with a Java captain, and the Azores follow, then squalls, high living, and strange sights: albatrosses like ships, seals like whales, and mirage lands. Slocum writes a plain, brave log of the first solo circumnavigation.
6328-the-junior-classics-volume-5-storie:
William Patten's fifth Junior Classics volume gathers stories that never grow old, for boys and girls, with an introduction by Charles W. Eliot of Harvard. Arabian Nights open the book, with Ali Baba and the forty thieves, Aladdin and his wonderful lamp, and Sindbad the sailor. Robinson Crusoe follows, shipwrecked, alone on a desolate island, building a boat, finding a footprint, and rescuing Friday from cannibals.

Gulliver's Travels gives Lilliput, giants, and an escape from an eagle, while E. Nesbit retells Shakespeare's plays, from Midsummer Night's Dream and The Tempest to As You Like It and The Merchant of Venice. Sindbad's ivory trading and caravan journey close the sample, with perils of sea, pirates, and serpents behind him. The volume is a treasury of tales retold for young readers, meant to last.
6411-round-the-world:
Andrew Carnegie first printed Round the World for private circulation, like his American Four in Hand in Britain. Publishers asked to give it to the public, and he revised it slightly, adding what general circulation required. Letters from strangers moved him most, including invalids who thanked him for making reading days pass, still coming almost daily when he wrote the preface.

Carnegie's journey runs through lands where emperors claim heaven's mandate, yet people claim the right to dethrone a bad emperor and even put him to death. An emperor, his people are told, is Son of Heaven, and he alone intercedes between his children and heaven. Carnegie writes travel as a rich man's diary, curious, opinionated, and fond of comparing governments as he circles the globe.
6425-flowing-gold:
Rex Beach dedicates Flowing Gold to his wife, sweetheart, and partner, whose faith and devotion never fail as inspiration. Room service at the Ajax, newest, largest, and most expensive hotel in Dallas, gives extra care to breakfast from the Governor's suite, most elegant of all. A waiter checks chilled fruit and hot plates before rapping, and a loud, cheery voice bids him enter, asking first where his cigarettes are.

Cold showers, the speaker calls an atrocious practice, a relic of barbarism and cruel shock to a languid nervous system. Later, a flushed, defiant man faces Gray, McWade, and Stoner, while a newcomer says a farce is done and the episode closed, so far as he is concerned. Beach writes an oil boom novel of hotels, money, and men, where gold flows fast and tempers faster, from Dallas suites to fields beyond.
6461-facing-the-world:
Horatio Alger Jr. gives Facing the World a hero whose parents have both died, left to an unjust and unkind guardian. In desperation the boy runs away and finds a true friend in a man who aids him and makes him his helper as a magician. They travel over the country with many interesting experiences, narrow escapes, and thrilling adventures, the preface promises. Harry receives a letter in chapter one, brought by round faced George Howard, aged ten.

Harry, five or six years older, lost his father a week before and stays with Mr. Benjamin Howard, a friend of his father, no relation. A mid scene shows Harry escaping his guardian's house, clipping Joel on the head, knocking him over, and running out while Mrs. Fox cries over her poor dear Joel. Alger writes a boy's rise story, where pluck, a friend, and a magician's road lead out of misfortune.
6664-the-story-of-a-child:
Pierre Loti, in a translation by Caroline Smith, tells the story of a child with a preface on the new study of child life. Child study is not new, the preface says; wise parents and kind teachers have always done it, but now folk try to do it with more system. Hopes that a new science would soon remake schooling have cooled, yet real gains remain.

Loti's tale itself follows a boy's inner world, with the wonder and fear that mark early years. His prose is tender and observant, far from dry theory. The Story of a Child is a gentle, classic memoir-novel, for readers who like to see the world through young eyes.
6704-a-domestic-problem-work-and-culture:
Mrs. A. M. Diaz asks a plain question in 1895: how may a woman enjoy the delights of culture and still meet her duties to family and household? Her chapters take a view of the situation, weigh woman's mission in two parts, prove culture a need for the child-trainer, and seek reasons for a change. A way out, lecture topics, and means already in use follow.

Diaz writes for women caught between books and housework, with sympathy and practical sense. Her aim is not revolt, but a better balance of mind and home. A Domestic Problem is a thoughtful, early feminist work, still relevant to readers who juggle learning and daily care.
6751-the-winds-of-the-world:
Talbot Mundy opens The Winds of the World with Yasmini's song, calling listeners to hear winds that fare east, west, south, and north, like shuttles weaving back and forth. Sightless touch and keen vision, she asks, can they learn where the winds have been, or what rumors mean? Wise men, the song says, harken, while fools shout and fail.

The tale that follows opens under a watery July sun on a Punjab skyline, with Indian cavalry in khaki and steel between British infantry and guns. Intrigue, war, and a mysterious woman drive the plot. The Winds of the World is a stirring, exotic adventure of India under the Raj.
680-the-golden-threshold:
Sarojini Naidu gathers her early poems in this volume, with an introduction by Arthur Symons and a dedication to Edmund Gosse. Folk songs lead the set: Palanquin-Bearers, Wandering Singers, Indian Weavers, Coromandel Fishers, and the Snake-Charmer. Songs for music and poems follow, from an ode to the Nizam of Hyderabad to Nightfall in the City of Hyderabad.

Naidu writes with musical, colorful verse, blending Indian scenes with English forms. Symons notes the earliest poems were read in London in 1896, when she was seventeen. The book endures as a landmark of Indian English poetry, where a young voice sings her homeland into verse.
6882-this-simian-world:
Clarence Day argues, with humor and pride, that people are apes at heart and should own that kinship rather than hide it. He traces his own line back through fish, worms, and dinosaurs to tree living forebears, and he prefers that wild ancestry to the pale pair of Eden. The book opens on a Sunday drive up Broadway, where vast crowds stroll, stare, and talk with no clear aim.

His friend Potter calls such masses vermin-like, since no other creature gathers in such aimless throngs. Day turns that jest into a wider look at human habits, asking what sets people apart from beasts and what does not. The result is a short, playful essay on pride, crowds, and our animal past.
7032-prose-idylls-new-and-old:
Charles Kingsley, canon of Westminster, gathers prose idylls new and old in this 1882 Macmillan edition. The contents list A Charm of Birds, Chalk Stream Studies, The Fens, My Winter Garden, From Ocean to Sea, and North Devon. The first idyll asks whether educated English folk are losing the old love for spring, which among forefathers rose almost to worship.

Budding leaves and returning songbirds once woke yearly astonishment, when the sun was a god sick each winter and returning in spring to life and glory. Kingsley writes of birds, streams, fens, and gardens with a naturalist's delight and a parson's warmth. The idylls blend outdoor observation with reflection on the changing year.
7166-the-home-and-the-world:
Bimala tells her own story, and she begins with her mother: the red mark in her hair, the wide-bordered sari, and eyes full of depth and peace. As a child she resented looking like her mother and blamed her mirror for her dark features, yet she also felt her mother's quiet holiness outshine mere prettiness. Rabindranath Tagore wrote the novel in Bengali, and Surendranath Tagore rendered it into English.

Memory drives the opening, moving from childhood hurt to a young woman's wish to live up to an epic ideal of womanhood. When a marriage proposal arrives, an astrologer reads her palm and finds good signs, hinting at the new life ahead. The voice stays close and plain, letting one woman's inner life carry the weight of the tale.
7814-daybreak-a-romance-of-an-old-world:
James Cowan's Daybreak, a Romance of an Old World, sends an astronomer royal and his companions from Earth to the Moon and Mars. Chapters promise a fallen satellite, two men in the Moon, one woman, an introduction to Mars, rapid transit there, and a prophet named Thorwald puzzled by new wonders.

Later headings bring more worlds than two, Mars as it is, Thorwald's home, a morning talk, Proctor showing Earth, a night adventure, and a search for Mona. Picture telegraphs, business ethics, and children's days mix with space travel, in a Victorian romance of science, faith, and other worlds.
7824-melody-the-story-of-a-child:
Laura E. Richards's Melody, dedicated to her sister Julia Romana Anagnos, opens with Miss Vesta praising a child's wonderful gift. Melody's voice pours through an open window like a wave of sound, and Miss Rejoice, lying abed, compares it to nightingales and skylarks in poetry books.

Contents run from the child and the doctor through the road, Rosin the Beau, the churchyard, the serpent, lost, waiting, Blondel, darkness, and light. Through a white lilac bush in June breeze and a road beyond, the book tells how a blind girl's song brings joy to a house and a town.
8456-patty-fairfield:
Carolyn Wells introduces Patty Fairfield in this girls' book. Its contents trace her story: her father's plan, traveling north, new friends, Villa Rosa, a minuet, and purple and fine linen. A sleigh ride, an absent-minded cousin, the Flemings, Patty's pranks, a book party, and home-made music follow. Patty, a lively girl, moves among relatives and friends, learning manners and mischief in turn.

Wells, a prolific children's author, wrote Patty as the first of a long series, and the book's charm lies in its heroine's high spirits. Readers of classic girls' fiction will find a wholesome, old-fashioned tale, where parties, pranks, and family feeling carry the plot. It suits young readers and nostalgic adults alike.
9176-queen-mary-and-harold:
Alfred, Lord Tennyson, Poet Laureate, bound two historical dramas in this volume. Queen Mary treats Mary Tudor, her Spanish husband Philip, and the men around her throne. Cardinal Pole, Cranmer, Gardiner, and Wyatt all take their parts. Harold tells of the Saxon king who fell at Hastings.

Tennyson writes in blank verse, aiming for truth of character over stage show. The plays ask how rulers bear faith, love, and power under fate. They remain valued as serious verse drama by England's great Victorian poet, and as a window on his view of history.
9651-a-child-world:
James Whitcomb Riley wrote A Child-World, a book of poems and tales of Indiana childhood. The proem paints a fairy paradise of dawns, dewdrops, orchard birds, and bees, a world long lost to grown eyes. Contents follow the old-home folks, Noey Bixler, the Loehrs and Hammonds, and an evening company. Florrety's music, heat lightning, and bewildering emotions fill the later pages.

Riley writes in Hoosier dialect and plain lyric, with humor and pathos in equal measure. His child world feels both real and dreamlike, a place of small wonders. A reader gets a fond, nostalgic book of youth, from America's best-loved Hoosier poet, rich in laughter and tender recall.
988-the-education-of-the-child:
Ellen Key, a Swedish writer on youth and the home, argues here for a new way to raise children. She rejects harsh drill, fear, and rote rules, and asks adults to watch each child and fit care to that child's bent. The plea grew out of late nineteenth-century debates on schooling, faith, and the rights of the young.

Key urges patience, play, fresh air, and work suited to a child's age, and she warns that threats crush the good they claim to guard. Faults, in her view, often hide a gift that wise care can draw out. Her short tract still speaks to parents and teachers who want firm guidance without breaking a child's spirit.
9926-the-two-guardians-or-home-in-this-w:
Charlotte Mary Yonge's 1871 novel follows young people placed under two guardians, and asks what a true home means in this world. Yonge, author of The Heir of Redclyffe, wrote for young readers with a clear moral purpose, and her preface explains the lesson she hoped to point.

The story moves through family life, friendship, and the small choices that shape character, with Marian at its center. Yonge's tone is earnest and domestic, and her interest lies in duty, patience, and faith. Readers who enjoy Victorian family stories will find her familiar blend of warmth and instruction.
a-domestic-problem-work-and-culture-in-t:
Mrs. A. M. Diaz published her study of the household in 1895, as her title page dates it, under two heads: work and culture. Her contents begin by taking a view of the situation: mistresses worn down by housekeeping, servants untrained and transient, and children raised by whoever can be hired. One cause, she argues, lies in a cramped idea of woman's mission.

Later chapters prove culture a need of the child-trainer, weigh other causes, and offer reasons for a change, a way out, and ways of immediate escape, ending with means already in operation. Diaz, a reformer and abolitionist of long standing, writes practically: cooperative housekeeping, training, and simpler living all get their hearing.
a-little-journey-in-the-world:
Charles Dudley Warner explains his title in an introductory sketch: he first thought of calling the story A Dead Soul, then dropped it to avoid confusion with Gogol. His aim, he says, is to trace the demoralization of a woman's soul by the influences of prosperous society. Margaret begins with the highest ideals.

Through a rich marriage and the world of fashion, money-making, and display, those ideals are eaten away step by step. Warner reflects her fall in the once pure mirror of her conscience, as he puts it. The novel is a Gilded Age moral tale, gentle in manner and serious in purpose, about what success costs the inner life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiquity-of-:
How old is the world, and how can anyone tell? That question frames a long survey of early attempts to date the earth and humankind. Physicists and geologists lead the two camps, one reading heat and spin, the other reading rock layers and fossils. Written in the early twentieth century, the survey weighs their rival figures before modern dating methods settled the debate.

Lord Kelvin heads the physics side, with estimates drawn from the slowing spin of the earth, its polar flattening, and the cooling of its crust. Other physicists put the age far lower, while geologists argued from sediment and erosion.
