Turning to human remains and tools, the survey closes near the Bible's own chronology, placing humankind at about ten thousand years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnauld:
Arnauld, also spelled Arnaut or Arnault, is a celebrated family whose history is bound up with Jansenism and Port-Royal. Originally from Auvergne, the family settled in Paris about the mid-sixteenth century, where several members made their names at the bar. Antoine Arnauld, who lived from 1560 to 1619, was a famous lawyer of the Paris assembly and a state counsellor under Henry IV. He is known for a 1594 speech for the University of Paris against the Jesuits and for political pamphlets.

His best known writing is a frank and true discourse of the king on restoring the Jesuits, published in 1602. By his marriage to Catherine Marion he had twenty children, ten surviving him, including Port-Royal nuns Angélique and Mother Agnès, and sons Arnauld d'Andilly, Henri, and Antoine. The long article follows the family in order of fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnold:
Arnold is the shared name of several medieval figures gathered in one entry, and the article sorts them briskly. Arnold Amalricus, Cistercian abbot of Cîteaux in 1201, inquisitor and legate in 1204, and archbishop of Narbonne in 1212, died in 1225. His alleged order to kill Catholics and Albigenses alike at Béziers in 1209 is amply refuted, the article notes, by Tamizey de Larroque.

Others include Arnold of Badeto, Dominican prior of Limoux and general inquisitor at Toulouse in 1531, author of works on the world's wonders and against heresy. Arnold of Bonneval was Benedictine abbot of Chartres from 1144 to 1156, correspondent and biographer of Bernard. Arnold of Cologne was second master architect of Cologne cathedral, succeeding Gerhard, whose work with his son John shaped that great church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustin-von-:
Augustin von Alfeld was one of the earliest and fiercest opponents of Luther. A Franciscan of the Regular Observance, he was born in the village of Alfeld near Hildesheim and died probably in 1532. Nothing is known of his youth, and his name is missing from the rolls of Erfurt, Rostock, Leipzig, and Wittenberg. He likely studied in a monastic school instead. By 1520 he was lector of Scripture at Leipzig, and at the Bishop of Merseburg's urging he opposed Lutheran teaching.

On 20 January 1521 he chaired a disputation at Weimar on monastic vows and life, whose outcome is lost, though it drew a satirical poem. He became Guardian at Halle in 1523 and Provincial of his Saxon province in 1529. A fluent Latinist, he knew Greek, Hebrew, and the classics, and his theology was medieval scholasticism. His writings were marred at times by bitterness and sarcasm, and Luther mocked him coarsely in return.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berthold:
Berthold, Bishop and Apostle of the Livonians, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Killed in 1198 during a crusade against the pagan Livonians, he had been abbot of the Cistercian monastery of Loccum in Hanover. On the death of Meinhard, first Bishop of Livonia, the Archbishop of Bremen named Berthold his successor.

The Livonians threatened Christians living in their territory, and Berthold came with an army as much as with a mission. He fell in battle on 24 July 1198, a bishop-martyr of the Baltic crusades. The entry presents a mission that turned to war, and a shepherd who died with his soldiers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-berch:
Blessed Berchtold, Abbot of Engelberg in Switzerland, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His birth date is unknown, and he died on 3 November 1197. A monk of Engelberg and favourite disciple of the learned Abbot Frowin, he was chosen successor on Frowin's advice when Frowin died in March 1178.

Following his master, Berchtold kept strict discipline by his own example and cared for his monks' spiritual and intellectual growth. He also secured the house's temporal welfare, winning tithes from the churches of Stanz and Buochs. Annals credit him with foretelling Barbarossa's death, and later tales tell of water turned to wine and a lake stocked with fish by his blessing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-richa:
Richard Thirkeld, an English mission priest, was executed at York in 1583 for reconciling the queen's subjects to the Catholic Church. A Queen's College, Oxford man, he was ordained at Reims in April 1579. He returned to minister around York and served as confessor to Margaret Clitheroe.

Arrested on the eve of the Annunciation in 1583, he was visiting a Catholic prisoner in York's Ousebridge prison. He openly confessed his priesthood to his captors and the mayor. Tried in his cassock and biretta, he heard a guilty verdict on 27 May and his sentence the next day. He spent his last night teaching fellow prisoners and his last morning strengthening those brought to the bar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercian-ab:
Fifteen miles south of Saint Polten in Lower Austria stands Lilienfeld, a Cistercian abbey founded by Leopold the Glorious, Margrave of Austria, in 1202. Its first monks came from Heiligenkreuz near Vienna. In time it grew into one of the richest and most influential houses in the empire, its abbots often serving as imperial councillors.

Abbot Matthew Kollweis turned the monastery into a fortress against the Turks advancing on Vienna, sheltering many fugitives. Joseph the Second decreed its suppression in 1789, and valuables were carried to Vienna, but his death halted the ruin and Leopold the Second reversed the decree. Fire ravaged the buildings in 1810, though the church escaped. In 1910 forty-nine choir monks formed the community under Abbot Justin Panschab.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dunkeld:
Dunkeld in Scotland was made the primatial see of the Columban Church about the middle of the ninth century. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how King Kenneth MacAlpine rebuilt the church and monastery of King Constantine's founding there, later ruined by Danes, and brought Saint Columba's relics to the place. For 865, the Annals of Ulster style the see's first holder as Bishop of Fortrenn, name of the southern Picts' kingdom.

He was also Abbot of Dunkeld, holding the sway once held by Iona over the other Columban houses of Scotland. Later the primacy moved to Abernethy and then to Saint Andrews, and Dunkeld fell to lay abbots. From one of them, Crinan, sprang Malcolm the Third and his successors on the Scottish throne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elizabeth-inc:
Elizabeth Inchbald was an English novelist, dramatist, and actress, born near Bury Saint Edmunds in 1753 and dead at Kensington in 1821. Daughter of John Simpson, a Catholic farmer, she longed from childhood to act, despite a speech impediment. In 1772 she left home for London and married Joseph Inchbald, actor and artist, playing Cordelia to his Lear and many other parts until she left the stage in 1789.

Her husband died in 1779, and her first play was accepted in 1782. She wrote more than a dozen plays, many of them adaptations, praised for vivid talk and fair-drawn characters though none ranks high. Her first novel, A Simple Story, came out in 1791 and won instant success as an early English novel of passion, told simply and with pathos. Nature and Art followed, milder in its revolutionary views, and still read by students of the eighteenth-century novel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frances-bedin:
Frances Bedingfeld, born in Norfolk in 1616 and dead at Munich in 1704, was superioress of the English Institute of Mary, a congregation for women founded at St. Omer in 1603. She and her eleven sisters all entered religious life. Sent abroad for schooling, she joined the institute at Munich, was professed in 1633, and became head of the Munich house after her sister Winefrid, the first superioress, died in 1666.

At the urging of Catherine of Braganza, wife of Charles II, Frances founded a house in London in 1669, opening a school for young women first at St. Martin's Lane and then at Hammersmith, living in secular dress under the name Mrs. Long. Hauled before a magistrate, she was freed through family influence but warned not to shelter priests or teach youth, a warning she disregarded. In 1677 she founded a second community at York, where she spent her later years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-harol:
Francis Harold, an Irish Franciscan and historical writer who died at Rome on 18 March 1685, spent his scholarly life between Prague and Rome. He taught theology for a time at the Irish College in Prague, then moved to Rome. There he spent his remaining years at the Irish Franciscan College of St. Isidore as librarian, guarding a collection that served Irish scholars in exile.

In 1662 he published at Rome, in two folio volumes, an epitome of the Annals of his uncle Luke Wadding, covering 1208 to 1540. A life of Wadding, prefixed and dedicated to Cardinal Francesco Barberini, was reprinted in 1731. He also wrote a life of Blessed Turibius Alfonso Mogrovejo, Archbishop of Lima, published in 1683. He also wrote a 1673 collection of documents on Peruvian councils and church affairs, Lima Limata, whose corrected copy survives in the Royal Irish Academy library.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-alo:
Frederick Weld, youngest son of an English landowner, became a leading figure in New Zealand politics and later governed three colonies. Born at Chideock Manor in 1823, he reached New Zealand in 1843, explored both islands, and was the first to climb the Awatere Valley and find the overland passes to Canterbury. He entered the House of Representatives in 1853 and became premier in 1864.

His chief policy ended double rule by governor and ministers during the Maori war: his cabinet asked Britain to pull its troops out so the colony could answer for its own affairs. He also pushed through the Waikato confiscation, a native rights bill, native land courts, and the question of Maori seats. After a year he resigned, then governed Western Australia, Tasmania, and Singapore in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-helmold:
Holstein historian Helmold, born before 1150 and dead about 1177, wrote the chronicle of the Wends at Bishop Gerold's suggestion. Schooled at Brunswick under Gerold and formed under Vicelinus, Apostle of the Wends, at Faldera, he ended as parish priest at Bosau on Plön lake.

His Chronica Slavorum shows how Christianity and German settlement gained ground among the Wends of eastern Holstein. Vicelinus gave self-sacrificing missions, the Oldenburg bishopric moved to Lübeck, German influence spread, and Wends were subdued and displaced. Westphalian and Dutch settlers summoned in. Early chapters lean on Adam of Bremen and Saxon records and run unreliable, but for his own time, drawn from Vicelinus and Gerold, he remains the chief source.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hersfeld:
Hersfeld was an ancient imperial abbey of Benedictines in Hesse-Nassau, standing where the Geisa and Haune join the Fulda. Sturmi, a disciple of St. Boniface, first founded a house here in 742 but moved it to Fulda for fear of Saxon attack. After the Franks beat the Saxons, Lullus, bishop of Mainz, re-founded the monastery about 768, and Charlemagne and other benefactors endowed it richly.

Relics of St. Wigbert brought pilgrims after 780, and a fine library, regular annals, and 150 monks made Hersfeld famed for piety and learning. Discipline slackened late in the tenth century, but St. Gotthard reformed the house and sent monks to revive other monasteries. In the long struggle between Emperor Henry IV and Pope Gregory VII, Hersfeld took the imperial side, as the entry goes on to show.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-wild:
Johann Wild, better known by his Latin name Ferus, was a Franciscan preacher whose sermons helped keep Mainz Catholic during the Reformation. Born in Swabia in 1497, he joined the Franciscans young, studied at Cologne, and won a reputation for deep knowledge of Scripture and the Fathers. In 1540 he became cathedral preacher at Mainz, a post he held until his death in 1554.

Even a Protestant historian called him the most learned preacher in sixteenth-century Germany, praising days and nights spent in sacred duties and study. When Albert of Brandenburg's troops sacked Mainz in 1552, Wild stayed while others fled, refused to give up his habit, and preached boldly before the prince himself. His one request, granted on the spot, was that the cathedral and Franciscan buildings be spared, and his commentaries on Scripture carried his influence far beyond the pulpit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-joseph-h:
John Joseph Hornyold was Vicar Apostolic of England's Midland District and author of popular explanations of the faith. Born in 1706 to two ancient Catholic families, he entered the English College at Douai at twenty-two and was ordained. He served at Grantham under persecution, more than once narrowly escaping arrest, before becoming chaplain at Longbirch in 1739.

There he published The Decalogue Explained in 1744, so approved that Oxford sent something like official thanks. It was followed by The Sacraments Explained in 1747 and The Real Principles of Catholics, a catechism for adults, in 1749. Chosen coadjutor to Bishop Stonor, he was consecrated in 1752 and stayed as chaplain to Madam Giffard until her death. He then lived in her house as vicar apostolic, ruling the Midland District zealously from 1756 until his death in 1778.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-macdonal:
John MacDonald of Glenaladale was a Scottish laird who mortgaged his estates to save his persecuted Catholic tenants by emigration. Born about 1742, he was educated at the Scots College in Ratisbon from 1756 and chosen tanister, or second in command, to his chief of Clanranald. It was an evil time for Catholic Jacobite Scotland, and a renegade landlord in South Uist drove tenants to choose between faith and home.

Hearing their plight, MacDonald went to investigate and resolved on heroic abnegation. Mortgaging his estates to his cousin, he bought land on Prince Edward Island in 1771. The next year the South Uist tenants sailed for Canada, with MacDonald following a year later. During the Revolutionary War he raised the 84th Royal Highland Emigrant Regiment with General Small. He was offered the island's governorship but barred by the Test Act as a Catholic, and served the new colonists until his death in 1811.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lajos-haynald:
Lajos Haynald (1816-1891) was Cardinal Archbishop of Kalocsa-Bacs in Hungary. Schooled at Pozsony, Nagyszombat, and Vienna, he took holy orders in 1839 and a theology doctorate in 1841, then taught at Gran's seminary from 1842.

Prince-Primate Kopacsy sent him abroad to study pastoral training and church administration, chiefly in Paris, likely the first Hungarian to do so. As chancellor-director in 1848, he refused to publish Hungary's independence declaration of April 1849 and lost his post, regaining it after the war. Coadjutor of Transylvania in 1851 and bishop in 1852, he championed Transylvania's union with Hungary, clashed with Vienna, resigned in 1864, worked in Rome, and became Archbishop of Kalocsa-Bacs in 1867.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lambert-of-he:
Lambert of Hersfeld (about 1024 to after 1077) was a medieval historian, a Benedictine of Hersfeld in Hesse from 15 March 1058, ordained priest that autumn at Aschaffenburg. Straight after ordination he slipped off to the Holy Land without his abbot's leave, returning in September 1059 to beg pardon from the dying Abbot Meginher.

Only once more did he leave home: fourteen weeks at Siegburg and Saalfeld in 1071. There he studied a reform from Fruttuaria in Piedmont, which he disliked against strict old Benedictine discipline. His Annales Lamberti run from creation to 1077. To 1040 they thinly copy older annals. To 1068 they grow fuller, resting on eyewitnesses. Then comes an elaborate Sallust-style history to 1077, long praised for truth until Ranke and later scholars charged him with bias and falsification.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lichfield:
The ancient diocese of Lichfield rose from St. Cedd and his companions' conversion of Mercia in 652. St. Chad later set his seat at Lichfield and built a monastery there. Lichfield grew in political weight until Offa resolved to raise it as a rival to Canterbury.

At Chelsea in 785 papal legates gave Bishop Higbert the pallium, with sway over Worcester, Leicester, Lincoln, Hereford, Elmham, and Dunwich. After the Conquest, the see's estates were laid waste, and Lichfield was so poor that after the Synod of 1075, Bishop Peter chose Chester. His successor Robert de Limesey moved the seat to Coventry. Roger de Clinton rebuilt its cathedral and rededicated it to St. Chad, whose relics he enshrined. Gregory IX (1227-1241) settled Lichfield-Coventry quarrels by ordering elections made alternately by each chapter. It holds the west front and the Lady Chapel, and stands alone in having three spires.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-gabriel:
Louis Gabriel Ambroise, Vicomte de Bonald, was a French statesman, writer, and philosopher, born near Millau in 1754 and dead at Paris in 1840. Schooled by Oratorians at Juilly, he served in the king's musketeers, became mayor of Millau in 1785, and sat in the Aveyron assembly in 1790.

Emigration and service in Conde's army followed. At Constance in 1797 he published his Theory of Political and Religious Power, banned in France. Back home under a false name, he wrote against divorce and for primitive law. He welcomed the Bourbon restoration, sat as deputy and peer, and in 1816 carried the law that abolished divorce in France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-jacques:
Louis Jacques Maurice de Bonald was a French cardinal and Archbishop of Lyons, born at Millau in 1787 and dead at Lyons in 1870. Fourth son of the philosopher Vicomte de Bonald, he studied at Saint-Sulpice, was ordained in 1811, and served Rome's concordat talks after the Restoration.

Bishop of Puy from 1823 for sixteen years, he rose to Lyons in 1839 and the cardinalate in 1841. His pastoral letters show a pious, eloquent, zealous bishop who fought Gallicanism and Jansenism, purged Lyons liturgical books, and crowned his discipline with a provincial synod in 1850. He also pleaded for flood victims, Spanish refugees, and silk workers in distress.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osbald:
Osbald was a Northumbrian noble whose brief kingship in 796 lasted only twenty-seven days. In 780 he joined another ealdorman in burning the house of Bearn, the king's justiciary, at Selectune. Alcuin wrote to him with Ethelred and Osberct in 793, urging them to shun the vices that had ruined earlier rulers.

When King Ethelred was murdered at Corbridge on 19 April 796, some nobles chose Osbald the patrician as king. His following deserted him, and he fled to Lindisfarne. Eardulf's exile then ended with recall and a York crowning in May. Alcuin wrote again to the fallen king at Lindisfarne, pressing him to give up worldly ambition and take up the monastic life. Osbald died in 799.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-sarsf:
Patrick Sarsfield was an Irish Jacobite soldier born at Lucan near Dublin about 1650 and dead at Huy in Belgium in 1693. Through his mother he descended from the O'Mores, princes of Leix, his grandfather Roger More having planned the 1641 rising, while his father came of Anglo-Norman stock. His father left him land worth 2,000 pounds sterling a year, and his elder brother married a natural daughter of Charles II.

Sarsfield first served as ensign in Monmouth's Foot in Luxembourg's army, but at Sedgemoor, where he was wounded, he fought for the king. In 1688 he trailed James II to France, then came back with him to Kinsale in 1689. James doubted his fitness for high command, yet Sarsfield took Sligo and secured Connaught in 1689. After the Boyne he helped hold Limerick, destroying William's siege train, the war's most brilliant exploit, before dying of wounds in Flanders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-theobal:
Theobald of Provins, born in Champagne in 1017, died at Salanigo in Italy on 30 June 1066. Of noble birth, he slipped away from his parents in 1054 with his friend Walter to live as hermits in the Ardennes and near Trier. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a pilgrim who never quite reached the Holy Land.

The two friends walked to Compostella in Spain and twice to Rome, then set out for Palestine by way of Venice, but Walter's strength failed near Salanigo and they settled there. After Walter died, disciples gathered around Theobald, the bishop ordained him priest, and even his mother stayed to live a religious life under his guidance. His shrine drew pilgrims long after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-henry-bed:
Henry Bedingfield, knight born in 1509 and dead in 1583, was grandson of Edmund Bedingfeld. He won from Edward IV a patent to fortify Oxburgh, hold a weekly market, and keep a piepowder court. With Henry Jerningham, Sir Henry chiefly placed Mary Tudor on the throne, proclaiming her at Norwich and winning a yearly pension of one hundred pounds from Wyatt's forfeited estates. 

As jailer of Princess Elizabeth, suspected in Wyatt's rebellion, he has been persistently misrepresented by Foxe and others. Yet his whole custodianship survives in letters to the queen and Privy Council, with their replies, published by the Norfolk and Norwich Archaeological Society. The correspondence fully clears him of cruelty or want of courtesy toward his royal captive. On Elizabeth's accession he retired to Oxburgh, still trusted enough to be asked for a horse and armed man against a feared French invasion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-henry-cha:
Henry Charles Englefield, antiquary and scientist born in 1752, died on 21 March 1822. Eldest son of the sixth baronet, he inherited White Knights and Wootton Bassett on his father's death in 1780. He never married and gave his whole life to study. At twenty-six, in 1778, he became a Fellow of the Royal Society, and the next year a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries, serving long as its vice-president and then as president.

As a Catholic he was barred from re-election as president and replaced by the Earl of Aberdeen. Under his direction the society produced from 1797 to 1813 its engravings of English cathedrals, to which he contributed papers on Durham, Gloucester, and Exeter. Besides antiquarian papers in Archaeologia, he worked in chemistry, mathematics, astronomy, and geology, winning the Society of Arts gold medal for his Discovery of a Lake from Madder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-springfield:
Springfield was a Massachusetts diocese erected in June 1870, covering five counties of the central and western state, Worcester, Hampden, Hampshire, Franklin, and Berkshire. This entry gives its area as 4,320 square miles, just over half the state, and its 1910 population as 843,212, of whom 323,122 were Catholics.

Its early history holds a striking detail: Puritan children captured at Deerfield and Westboro, carried to Canada. And raised Catholic married there, and one descendant, Joseph-Octave Plessis, became Archbishop of Quebec in 1806. The entry follows the diocese from those tangled beginnings through parishes and institutions, a portrait of Catholic New England growing beside old Puritan towns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alfwold:
St. Alfwold, or Aelfwold, was bishop of Sherborne in Dorset, dying in 1058, and this entry draws its few details from William of Malmesbury. A monk of Winchester, he was consecrated bishop of Sherborne in 1045, succeeding his own brother Brightwy. And won admiration by the frugality of his life, in sharp contrast to the riotous banqueting that Danish kings had made fashionable.

Devout to St. Swithun, his old Winchester patron, and to St. Cuthbert, whose shrine at Durham he visited on pilgrimage, he died while singing Cuthbert's antiphon. Strictly speaking he was Sherborne's last bishop, since after his death the see joined Ramsbury, and the entry preserves a modest, disciplined prelate at the end of an era.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-erconwald:
Erconwald, bishop of London until about 690, spent his own fortune on monasteries before he spent his authority on a diocese. Of the princely East Anglian house of Offa, he founded Chertsey for monks and Barking in Essex for nuns, placing his sister Ethelburga over the latter. He served as superior at Chertsey until Bishop Wini's death in 675 called him to London. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 notes King Sebbi and Archbishop Theodore backed his appointment.

Renowned for holiness, he was said to heal the sick through contact with his litter, on Bede's testimony. In 686 he witnessed Theodore's reconciliation with Wilfrith, and King Ini's laws call him my bishop. He enlarged his church, grew its revenues, and won it royal privileges. The entry joins monastic founder and diocesan builder in one career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ethelwold:
Ethelwold, bishop of Winchester from 963 to 984, drove the monastic reform of tenth-century England with a lion's severity and a dove's gentleness. Born at Winchester early in the century, he served at Athelstan's court, took the tonsure under Elphege the Bald, and was ordained priest alongside Dunstan. As dean at Glastonbury under Dunstan he was called a mirror of perfection. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 1 August 984.

Consecrated by Dunstan, he joined Dunstan and Oswald of Worcester against corruption spread by Danish inroads. At Winchester he replaced ill-living seculars with monks and refounded the ancient nunnery. His work reached Chertsey, Milton, Ely, Peterborough, and Thorney, expelling the unworthy and rebuilding houses. Father of monks and benevolent bishop sum up his fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ewald:
The two Ewalds, Northumbrian priests martyred in Old Saxony about 695, are remembered as Black and Fair for hair and complexion. Both studied for years in Irish schools, and Ewald the Black was the more learned, though both matched in holiness. Stirred by Willibrord's zeal for the Germans, they entered Saxon country about 690, in modern Westphalia. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 lodges them first with a Saxon earl's steward.

Suspected and condemned, they died at Aplerbeck, so the account runs, on 3 October. Ewald the Fair fell quickly by the sword, while the bolder, spokesman Black was torn limb from limb. Their bodies, cast into the Rhine, floated forty miles upstream to their companions, crowned by a pillar of light. The earl avenged them by fire and sword. The entry preserves a mission cut short and honoured.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gerald:
Gerald, bishop of Mayo, founded the monastery called Mayo of the Saxons for English monks in Ireland. An English monk of unknown birth, he followed Colman from Whitby's synod of 664 to Ireland and settled at Innisboffin in 668. When Irish and English monks fell out, Colman founded a separate house for thirty English brethren, with Gerald as first abbot in 670. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 13 March 731.

Bede, writing that very year, describes Mayo as still held by English monks living by their hands' labour, chaste and single, under rule and canonical abbot. Young as he was, Gerald ruled wisely until 697, when he is said to have resigned for Adamnan. Some hold Adamnan kept Roman Easter at Mayo in 703 before moving to Skreen. The entry preserves an English colony's monastic life on Irish ground.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hermengild:
Hermengild, Visigothic prince who died in 585, turned a family quarrel over faith into revolt and martyrdom. He was son of the Arian king Leovigild by his Catholic first wife Theodosia. In 576 he married Ingundis, a Frankish Catholic princess. His own bent, his wife, and Leander of Seville's teaching brought him into the Catholic fold. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 13 April 585.

His stepmother Goswintha, a fierce Arian, hated Ingundis and ill-treated her to force apostasy. Hermengild withdrew with his father's leave to Andalusia with his wife. When Leovigild learned of the conversion, he called his son to Toledo. Hermengild disobeyed. Angered by his stepmother's zeal and his father's harsh rule over Spanish Catholics, he took arms for his fellow believers and his own rights, allying with Byzantium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-oswald:
Oswald, archbishop of York, drove the tenth-century monastic revival in England beside Dunstan and King Edgar. Of Danish parentage, he was raised by his uncle Odo of Canterbury and taught by Fridegode. After serving as dean of secular canons at Winchester, he sought a stricter life at Fleury in France and was ordained there.

Returning in 959, he became bishop of Worcester in 962 and, with Edgar's backing, replaced secular canons with monks at Worcester, Winchcombe, Pershore, and Westbury. His most famous foundation was Ramsey, whose church was dedicated in 974. Made archbishop of York in 972, he journeyed to Rome for the pallium and died on 29 February 992.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-romuald:
Romuald, founder of the Camaldolese, fled a duel's horror into a hermit's life of extreme austerity. Born at Ravenna probably about 950, though Peter Damian claimed he lived to one hundred and twenty, he spent his youth in a noble's thoughtless pleasures. At twenty, horrified because his father killed an enemy in a duel, he fled to San Apollinare in Classe.

That house, reformed by Maiolus of Cluny, still seemed too lax, and his rebukes stirred enmity. He retired to Venice under the hermit Marinus, then founded hermitages and monasteries across Italy, blending solitary cells with community life. The Camaldolese order bears his mark. He died at Val di Castro on 19 June 1027, and the entry disputes Damian's inflated age with modern criticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-willibald:
Willibald and Winnebald were Benedictine brothers from Wessex, children of St Richard the King and kin of Boniface. Willibald entered Waltham abbey at five, and pilgrimaged to Rome with his father and brother in 722. After his father's death at Lucca, he set out for the Holy Land in 724, reaching Jerusalem in November 725.

By way of Tyre and Constantinople he reached Monte Cassino in 730, returned to Rome in 740, and was sent by Gregory III to Germany. Boniface ordained him in 741 and made him bishop of Eichstätt. Winnebald, priest in Thuringia from 740, attended the great German councils and became abbot of Heidenheim, where his sister Walburga ruled the women's house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synod-of-bacc:
The Synod of Baccanceld met at Bapchild near Sittingbourne in Kent in 694, though it was more a parliament, a witenagemot, than a church synod. King Wihtred of Kent presided, with Archbishop Brihtwald of Canterbury, Bishop Tobias of Rochester, abbots, abbesses, priests, deacons, and lay lords present. Its chief enactments stand in a charter securing the Church's gifts and privileges forever.

What had once been given to God, the charter held, might never return to human use. On a prelate's death, fitting successors were to be chosen with the archbishop's advice and approval, without royal meddling, and lay interference was disclaimed outright. Canterbury and Rochester gained perpetual freedom from royal requisitions except voluntary gifts. Spelman regarded the charter as the most ancient in England, and its general terms are judged genuine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-abbey-of-:
The Abbey of Bursfeld, west of Göttingen on the Weser, ranked among Germany's celebrated medieval Benedictine monasteries. Duke Henry of Nordheim and his wife Gertrude founded it in 1093 and endowed it richly, and Henry IV granted privileges. Its first abbot, Almericus, came from Corvey with monks and opened a school that soon grew famous under the next four abbots. In 1331, under Abbot Henry Lasar, discipline relaxed, the school languished, and riches were dissipated.

From 1331 to 1424 no records survive. When Albert of Bodenstein became abbot in 1424, church and school lay in ruins and only one monk remained. Too old for the task, he resigned in 1430. Reforming zeal then swept the Catholic world, and John Dederoth, reformer of Clus, took up Bursfeld in 1433 at Duke Otto's urging. With four monks from St Matthias, he restored the house beyond expectation, founding the Bursfeld Congregation that reformed Benedictine houses widely.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theobald:
Canterbury's archbishop Theobald, who died on 18 April 1161, is the Norman prelate portrayed here. He took Benedictine vows at Bec toward the close of the eleventh century or the start of the twelfth, becoming prior in 1127 and abbot in 1137. Election as archbishop followed on 28 December 1138, consecration on 8 January next, and a Roman journey for his pallium took him to the Second Lateran Council.

Wise, capable, devout in private, charitable, and a lover of learning, he backed Stephen in civil war, crowning him, while working always for Angevin succession. His household gathered able young men, including successor Thomas of Canterbury. First to bring civil law into England, he founded a Canterbury law school under jurist Roger Vacarius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Greifswald holds the oldest university of Prussia, founded in 1456, though the town had briefly hosted one before. In 1436, when the Council of Basle placed Rostock under interdict over town dissensions, the university moved to Greifswald with the council's consent and stayed seven years. After its return to Rostock, six professors remained behind, and the burgomaster Heinrich Rubenow, himself a doctor of laws, conceived a university for his native city.

Pope Callistus III gave the bull of foundation on 29 May 1456, and the dedication took place on 17 October, with Rubenow as vice-chancellor and first rector's deputy. The entry follows the university through the Reformation, when it turned Lutheran, and through Swedish and Prussian rule, noting its faculties, endowments, and scholars across four centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valleyfield:
Valleyfield is a thriving Quebec city of about 10,000 people at the outlet of Lake St Francis on the St Lawrence's south shore. Founded in 1855 as St Cecilia, it became legally known in 1874 as Salaberry of Valleyfield. Its first pioneers were mostly fishermen and lumbermen. Today it has grown into a manufacturing centre for cotton, paper, bronze, and powder, powered by one of Quebec's finest water powers.

The Diocese of Valleyfield, erected on 5 April 1892, covers the counties of Beauharnois, Chateauguay, Huntingdon, Vaudreuil, and Soulanges. Its first and present bishop is Joseph-Médard Emard, born at St Constant in 1853, trained at St Thérèse and Montreal seminaries, and ordained priest in 1880. The entry sketches the diocese's parishes, clergy, and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-al:
Thomas Alfield, also called Aufield or Badger, was an English priest executed at Tyburn in 1585. Educated at Eton and Cambridge, he converted, studied at Douai, and was ordained after the college moved to Reims. Sent to England in 1581, he worked with the mission of Edmund Campion and Robert Persons, chiefly in the north.

Arrested and sent to the Tower in 1582, he first confessed boldly under torture, then lapsed to the Protestant church after release. Repentant, he returned to Reims for fresh resolve. Back in England he risked his life circulating Cardinal Allen's defence of Catholics, with help from a dyer, Thomas Webley. Arrested again, he was hanged with Webley, while a reprieve for Alfield arrived too late.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-ma:
Thomas Maxfield, born in Stafford gaol about 1590, was a priest of a staunchly recusant family, Catholics who refused the established church. His father had been condemned for harbouring priests. Thomas trained at Douai, returned through ill health, then went back, was ordained, and reached London in 1615.

Within three months he was arrested and held at the Gatehouse, Westminster. A midnight escape by rope failed, and he spent seventy hours in the stocks in a filthy dungeon. Condemned at the Old Bailey solely for being a priest, he was taken to Tyburn on 1 July 1616. The Spanish ambassador had pleaded in vain for a pardon, and devout Spaniards joined the procession as a guard of honour around a gallows decked with garlands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wibald:
Wibald was a twelfth-century abbot and imperial statesman, born near Stavelot in Belgium in 1098 and dying at Bitolia in Paphlagonia in 1158 while returning from an embassy to Constantinople. Educated at Stavelot and Liège, he entered the Benedictines at Waulsort in 1117, headed its school. In 1130 was elected Abbot of Stavelot and Malmedy, adding Corvey in 1146, with Fischbeck and Kemnade annexed to Corvey months later.

Under Wibald, Stavelot reached its greatest fame and Corvey's declining discipline was restored. He ranked among the most influential counsellors of Emperors Lothair and Conrad III. He accompanied Lothair to Italy in 1137 and, through imperial influence, was elected Abbot of Monte Cassino. Resigned after only forty days when King Roger of Sicily threatened to destroy the monastery unless he did so. Under Conrad all imperial negotiations with Rome passed through his hands, and he visited Rome eight times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-clark:
William Clarkson Stanfield was an English painter of sea scenes who began life as a sailor and stage painter. Born at Sunderland in 1793, he died at Hampstead in 1867. A voyage to New Guinea brought friendship with the abolitionist Thomas Clarkson, whose name he added to his own. Disabled in 1816, he painted scenery for a sailors' theatre, then won London stage work and, on friends' advice, tried panel pictures.

He showed with the Society of British Artists in 1824 and 1827, reached the Academy in 1829, won a fifty-guinea prize, and gave up stage work for a Continental tour. From then he sent nearly one hundred and forty pictures to Academy shows. His canvases kept a showy, stage-like flair, but many charmed viewers, and his sea pieces rank among the finest of their kind. A devout Catholic, he spent his last years in an old Hampstead house.
desert-gold:
Zane Grey calls Desert Gold a romance of the border, and its contents promise flight into the desert, Yaqui fighters, white horses, and a secret at Forlorn River. Dick Gale, a young Easterner gone west, joins ranger Ladd and the Mexican girl Mercedes Castaneda in flight from the bandit Rojas. Cameron's haunted memories open the prologue.

The party crosses cactus and lava country, finds water and danger in equal measure, and uncovers what Forlorn River hides. Grey loads the landscape with heat, color, and pursuit, while the love story grows between Gale and Mercedes. Published in 1913, the novel helped fix the modern Western's desert mythology for millions of readers.
doctor-marigold:
Charles Dickens wrote Doctor Marigold as a Christmas story told by a Cheap Jack, a traveling salesman of crockery and hardware, whose father was Willum Marigold, never William. The narrator defends his father's name with a free country's logic before telling his life. He marries, loses his wife's love to her temper, and sees his deaf-mute daughter Sophy as his joy.

On a fortunate night he buys the child Mim from a brutal showman, beating a gong between Pickleson's publics, and raises the two girls together. Dickens performed this monologue on his reading tours to great effect. Its patter, half sales talk and half confession, shows his ear for street speech and his sentiment at full stretch.
doe-osti-2586798-determining-the-transie: Transient electric fields in repetitive pulses got determined, and this DOE report covers the pulse frequency effects. The pages detail the measurements. The plasma folks get their data. The fields were transient electric. The frequency was pulse repetition. The folks were plasma.
doe-osti-3014370-investigations-in-nucle: Nucleon spin got investigated, and this DOE text covers cold nuclear matter. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their data. The matter was cold nuclear. The data were physicist. The spin was nucleon. The data were DOE's. The matter was nuclear.
doe-osti-3018683-enhancing-a-lartpc-with: LArTPC got magnetically enhanced, and this DOE text adds the field. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their data. The field was magnetic. The data were physicist. The TPC was LAr. The enhancement was magnetic. The DOE was text.
facing-the-world:
Facing the World, by Horatio Alger Jr, gives its hero the author's standard beginning. The preface states it plainly. The boy's parents are both dead. His appointed guardian is unjust and unkind. In desperation he runs away. A true friend finds him, a traveling magician who makes the boy his helper. They tour the country together, with narrow escapes and thrilling adventures.

Harry receives his first letter in chapter one, at the Howards' house, a week after his father's funeral. He is sixteen, alone in the world, and already polite about it. Alger wrote this formula more than a hundred times without exhausting its market. Pluck, honesty, and a patron's timely friendship carry Harry as they carried all the bootblacks and newsboys before him. The magician is a new patron's costume. The gospel underneath never changes: the world rewards the boy who faces it squarely.
flowing-gold:
Flowing Gold, by Rex Beach, opens in the Governor's suite of the Ajax, Dallas's newest and most expensive hotel. Beach lavishes attention on the breakfast service. Chilled fruit must be chilled and hot plates hot. The pajama clad guest demands his cigarettes first of all. Cold showers, he declares, are a relic of barbarism. A hygienic, stimulating cigarette serves the same purpose without the shock.

Beach dedicates the novel to his wife, his sweetheart and partner, in a full page inscription. The flowing gold of the title is Texas oil. Dallas in a boom is the author's Alaska moved south. Beach made his name with The Spoilers and the Klondike. The same machinery turns here: sudden wealth, strong men, hotel suites, and love tested by money. The oil fields replaced the gold creeks. The fever, he suggests, is identical, and so is the cure.
following-the-equator-a-journey-around-t:
Mark Twain wrote this travel book out of the lecture tour that took him around the world in 1895 and 1896, a trip made to pay his debts. The Hartford title page gives his real name, Samuel L. Clemens, under the pen name. Each chapter opens with a maxim from Pudd'nhead Wilson's calendar, and the contents read like the voyage itself.

The party crosses America to Vancouver, sails to Honolulu, and crosses the equator to Fiji and Australia. Twain reports on Kanaka recruiting for Queensland plantations, convict discipline in early Sydney, and the fauna of Australasia, platypus included. India, South Africa, and the long road home fill the later chapters. Observation and tall talk alternate: few pages pass without a history lesson smuggled in as a joke.
friends-and-neighbors-or-two-ways-of-liv:
T. S. Arthur edited Friends and Neighbors; Or, Two Ways of Living in the World in Philadelphia in 1856. The title page names Arthur as editor, and his preface explains the gathering. Its pieces were gathered from many corners of current literature. Fitting sentiments by other hands open the volume.

The two ways of living are selfishness and kindness, shown through tales and sketches of ordinary folk. Neighbours help or hinder each other across fences, shops, and sickrooms. Arthur's editorial hand favours pieces where small generosities change a household's weather. The collection belongs to his long campaign for domestic virtue in popular print. Readers of his novels will know the tone: plain, warm, and certain that character shows itself at home first. It preserves a parlour anthology of the eighteen-fifties at work.
girls-new-and-old: Girls New and Old, by L, t, meade, the girls' tales. This book preserves that collection. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
govdocs-archive_org-alistTheManWhoMisrul:
Emanuel M. Josephson, a New York physician and pamphleteer, wrote Rockefeller Internationalist: The Man Who Misrules the World as an attack on the Rockefeller family's power. He had earlier written The Strange Death of Franklin D. Roosevelt, and he dedicated this book to the Constitution.

Josephson argues that the Rockefellers used their wealth, their foundations, and their international ties to rule America from behind the scenes. The book mixes documented material with sweeping charges, in the manner of mid-century conspiracy literature. It is held as an archive item, without endorsement, as a lasting source for the era's anti-Rockefeller feeling.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AgentOswaldAddr: Lee Harvey Oswald's address book became an exhibit in the Kennedy assassination investigation, its names and numbers checked one by one for what they revealed about his contacts. Among its entries was the name and number of FBI agent James Hosty, a detail that fueled decades of argument. This file holds the address book material as captured in the government releases. It is kept as issued, a small personal object turned into evidence in the most examined murder case in American history.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BuschowAA_Bus_R:
On December 7, 1963, two weeks after the assassination, the FBI filed this report concerning A. A. Buschow. It belongs to the Bureau's work on the route Lee Harvey Oswald took after leaving the Texas School Book Depository.

Oswald's movements between the shooting and his capture at the Texas Theatre were reconstructed minute by minute: the bus he boarded, the taxi he took, the rooming house he reached. Reports like this one checked the people along that route, drivers and passengers whose names surfaced in the canvass. The single report is preserved as part of that reconstruction file.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DorlandHarold_D: Harold Dorland wrote an essay, in letter form, on the subject of official history. The piece questions the accounts that governments and institutions publish about their own past actions. The surviving record identifies the author and his theme but gives no date or addressee, so the text stands as one writer's argument against taking official versions of events at face value.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KRLD_KRLD: A letter from 1967 thanks its recipient for a letter of December 1 and discusses a broadcast appearance made by telephone. The writer notes regular appearances on CBS stations. The author's name is garbled in the text and cannot be recovered. Radio letters like this one arranged the phone interviews through which assassination researchers reached audiences far from home.
