govdocs-archive_org-the-last-hours-of-eu: Adriano Romualdi's The Last Hours of Europe opens on the Soviet-German campaigns of the Second World War. He treats that eastern struggle as the turning point of Europe's fate. Romualdi, an Italian historian, writes the war as an elegy for a civilization ending. The book serves readers of his work and of the European right's memory of the war, in which defeat in the east closed an age.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
In 1971 a top Air Force official addressed the Joint Chiefs of Staff on the arithmetic of nuclear war. William Burr edited this briefing book around his shocking sentence. America could lose two hundred million people, the official said, and still have more than it had at the time of the Civil War.

Evidence here gives the quote, year, and editor, and little more. The quote alone explains the posting. Senior officers discussed national survival in percentages that treated hundreds of millions of deaths as an acceptable ledger entry. Preserving the sentence in context lets readers judge Cold War planning in its authors' own arithmetic.
her-weight-in-gold:
Her Weight in Gold, by George Barr McCutcheon, gathers nine stories first printed in magazines. New York published the volume in 1914. McCutcheon thanks the editors of the Saturday Evening Post and Good Housekeeping in his front matter. The title tale opens in society conversation. How much does she weigh, Eddie Ten Eyck asks. General Horatio Gamble has just declared, in desperation, that a certain lady is worth her weight in gold.

Satire turns that compliment into a bargain. The collection then ranges widely. The Maid and the Blade offers romance. Mr Hamshaw's Love Affair and The Green Ruby follow. The Gloaming Ghosts supplies a doubtful haunting. When Girl Meets Girl, Quiddlers Three, The Late Mr Taylor, and The Ten Dollar Bill complete the volume. McCutcheon, the Graustark novelist, works here at magazine length. Rich men, determined women, jewels, and phrases taken literally drive the plots.
light-on-the-path-and-through-the-gates-:
Mabel Collins wrote down these rules for disciples seeking wisdom. This edition reprints the 1888 George Redway text verbatim. Author's notes, first printed then, accompany the treatise. Comments come from Lucifer magazine, volumes from 1887 and 1888.

Through the Gates of Gold, from 1887, joins it here. William Q. Judge's commentary from The Path appears alongside. The rules demand killing ambition and desire of life first. Eyes must lose tears before they can truly see, Collins writes. Kill out desire of greatness, the rules continue in sequence. The soul's feet must wash in the heart's blood, Collins writes.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
A bound 1885 Lippincott's volume gathers half a year of issues. Old Series Volume Thirty-Six equals New Series Volume Ten. J. B. Lippincott Company published it in Philadelphia. Its contents list runs from The Art of Reading onward.

Grace R. Peirce, Mary Agnes Tincker, and Susan Hartley Swett contribute. A Chapter of Mystery by Charles Morris promises puzzles. General Grant at Frankfort appears among the nonfiction pieces. Fiction, poems, and letters fill out the half-year's reading. Joseph Mickley, the Lady Lawyer's first client, and muster-day appear. Letters of Charles Reade continue through the half-year's contents.
lord-of-the-world:
Robert Hugh Benson opens this novel with a prologue conversation. Percy waits while old Mr. Templeton leans back to speak. Templeton's silent room lies forty feet below the Thames embankment. The world began burrowing underground sixty years before, Benson writes.

A station of the Second Central Motor-circle stands one hundred yards away. Volor stations and artificial sunlight furnish this future London. Green jade-enamel lines the windowless, doorless room throughout. Three books, The Advent, The Encounter, and The Victory, structure it. Templeton seldom left his commodious underground house anymore. Board of Health enamel and classical frieze gratings ventilate it.
marmion-a-tale-of-flodden-field:
Marmion is Sir Walter Scott's tale of Flodden Field, in Cassell's 1888 library edition. An introduction tells how the poem was begun in November 1806. Constable offered a thousand guineas for it unseen. Miller and Murray eagerly joined the venture.

Scott's first romance, The Lay of the Last Minstrel, had triumphed in 1805. Now he took more than usual pains, and enjoyed the writing. His hero Marmion is a splendid, false-hearted knight. The tale runs through castles and convents to Flodden's battlefield. There, in 1513, Scotland's king and flowers fell together. Marmion's speed and color made Scott the age's favorite poet. Its best lines are quoted still.
masters-of-the-guild:
Louise Lamprey wrote Masters of the Guild, printed in New York in 1920. Florence Choate and Elizabeth Curtis drew the pictures. Lamprey had told guild tales before, in In the Days of the Guild.

Peirol of the Pigeons leads, with a tale of Bellerophon tucked inside. A tournament in the clouds and a set of puppet players follow. Padraig of the scriptorium copies books in his tale. A tapestry chamber and a castle tale round out the old world scenes. To Dorothy heads the contents, as a gift note to a child. Guild crafts, music, and art give each tale its bright core.
matthew-arnold: George Saintsbury wrote Matthew Arnold for the Modern English Writers set. William Blackwood and Sons printed it in Edinburgh and London. The copy here is a third impression, marked with the year 1902. Saintsbury held the chair of rhetoric and English letters at Edinburgh. The hosted sample preserves only the title page and the series list. No readable chapter text appears in it, so this note stays with those front page facts.
melody-the-story-of-a-child:
Laura E. Richards wrote Melody: The Story of a Child in 1894. She gave the book to the memory of her sister. Julia Romana Anagnos is named in that tender dedication.

Eleven chapters trace the child from The Child to Light. The Doctor, On the Road, and Rosin the Beau come early. A churchyard, a serpent, and a lost child darken the middle. Waiting and Blondel lead toward the last two heads, Darkness and Light. A line from Sidney Lanier heads the contents page. Child grief and child hope shape the short arc of the tale.
miss-mcdonald:
Mrs. Mary J. Holmes built this novel largely out of journals and letters. The contents open with extracts from Frances Thornton's journal, then Guy's, then Daisy's. An author's story interrupts the diaries, followed by a chapter called The Divorce. Five years later, the tale resumes with Daisy's letter and a visit to Saratoga.

Holmes was a bestselling author of domestic novels like Millbank and Ethelyn's Mistake. Here she lets three diarists tell one tangled story from three sides. A sick-room scene and the late chapter named Miss McDonald bring the threads together. The form suits her readers, who liked confession, courtship, and consequence.
my-days-and-nights-on-the-battle-field:
Charles Carleton Coffin wrote this Civil War book for young readers. Dana Estes issued it in Boston, copyrighted in 1887. Coffin had written Boys of '76 and Following the Flag. The book opens with a note to the youth of the United States.

Chapter one asks how the Rebellion came about. Coffin had reported the war from the field himself. His title promises days and nights spent on battlefields. He tells of marches, fights, and the men who bore them. The book taught a new generation the war their fathers fought, in plain words meant to stir memory and pride.
nasa-tm-19660007963-models-of-the-earth-:
Joseph C Cain at Goddard presented these models of Earth's magnetic field in Bergen, Norway, on August 16, 1965, and dated the paper October 1. A field model is a formula that gives the field's strength and direction anywhere. Cain builds the core field model from magnetometer data gathered on land and at sea, per the catalog note.

Good models serve navigation, geology, and spacecraft work alike. They also reveal slow changes in the deep field over time. Cain spoke at an institute on radiation trapped in the field. That link is practical: trapped particle paths are traced through the very field his models describe for other users.
nasa-tm-19660010209-recent-measurement-o:
J P Heppner reported recent satellite measurements of the magnetic field far from Earth in this Goddard paper. The data came from the EGO-1 satellite, also called OGO-A in the catalog note. The outer magnetosphere and its boundary regions are the areas covered. There, Earth's field is stretched and pressed by the solar wind, and its shape was still being mapped.

Field readings from a satellite in that region test every model. The boundary moves with solar conditions, so single readings can mislead. Heppner gathers recent results into one report for other workers. Such compilations let the next team plan orbits and instruments with the newest map of near-Earth space in hand.
nasa-tm-19670009023-earth-s-magnetic-fie:
Harold L. Stolov, of the Goddard Institute for Space Studies in New York, wrote this survey of Earth's magnetic field. It opens with the compass needle, the simplest proof of the field, and with William Gilbert, who first grasped the field's global character. Gilbert's 1600 treatise argued, from experiments with a spherical lodestone, that Earth itself is a great magnet.

About ninety percent of the main field, Stolov notes, matches a short dipole at Earth's center. The dipole tilts about eleven and a half degrees from the rotation axis. The survey recalls the first measurements of compass deviation in the sixteenth century and the first world charts of declination. The catalog record lists the wider topics covered: the dipole field, the magnetosphere, quiet-day geomagnetic variations, and dynamo theory for the ionosphere's origin.
nasa-tm-19680010616-theoretical-study-of:
Y. C. Whang, of the Laboratory for Space Sciences at Goddard Space Flight Center, models the Moon's shadow in space in January 1968. The solar wind cannot pass through the Moon, so a long, quiet wake trails behind it. Inside that wake, the magnetic field bends in ways worth predicting.

Whang builds a model for the field's disturbances in the plasma shadow. He solves Maxwell's equations directly for steady solutions. The disturbance is blamed on three kinds of drift currents in the plasma. His computed field changes match what the Explorer 35 satellite actually saw. The agreement backs the model's picture of the wake.
nasa-tm-19690028319-an-analysis-of-the-d:
Winifred Sawtell Cameron and George J. Coyle, of Goddard Space Flight Center, analyze boulder distribution near small lunar craters in this August 1969 preprint. Impacts scatter rocks inside and around the craters they blast out. A casual impression said the patterns differ by crater type. The pair set out to test that impression with statistics instead of eyeballing.

They inspected Lunar Orbiter III photographs from three lunar regions with a magnifying lens. Six hundred three craters wider than about a hundred meters entered the survey. Each crater's boulders were classed as spread far out, held within the crater and its rim, or not visible at all. The sites included ground near the Ranger and Surveyor landing zones.
now-it-can-be-told:
Philip Gibbs named his war book Now It Can Be Told, and its preface explains the title. Parts cover observers and commanders, the school of courage, and the nature of a battle. A winter of discontent, the heart of a city, and psychology on the Somme follow. The fields of Armageddon and for what men died close the plan.

Gibbs writes of aspects of the war the world must know and remember, he says. The book stands as a memorial of men's courage in tragic years. It also warns that war will happen again if evil and folly stay in peoples' hearts. He claims his daily reports from the western front stood truthful and accurate.
old-love-stories-retold:
Richard Le Gallienne retold famous love stories in prose. The hosted text holds one story from the book. That story treats poet Heinrich Heine and his Mathilda. The Gutenberg note says only this chapter is present. It warns readers that the file is partial.

His graceful hand gives the tales a tender tone. Readers of the hosted text get the Heine story alone. They should not expect the full printed collection here. Even alone, the piece shows his literary style. The file came out in June 2002 as text 3267. Volunteers typed it for free reading by all, it says.
patty-fairfield:
Patty Fairfield opens Carolyn Wells's Patty series, and it begins with a question. Patty's father asks her age, and she answers that she is fourteen. A plan of his sends her travelling north to stay with relatives and learn from households unlike her own.

The contents promise visits at Villa Rosa and Vernondale, a minuet, a sleigh-ride, a book party, and Patty's pranks. An absent-minded cousin and a funny family supply the comedy. The book is a cheerful girls' story about a lively heroine being polished by travel, company, and other people's ways of living.
pioneers-and-founders-or-recent-workers-:
Charlotte Mary Yonge gathered lives of noted mission workers in Pioneers and Founders, published by Macmillan in London in 1874. She aimed to show the character and growth of mission work over the last two centuries. She does this through single lives, from John Eliot's work among Native Americans onward.

Yonge states plainly what she leaves out. The Jesuit missions in Japan, China, and the Americas are set aside. So are the Moravian missions in Greenland, the United States, and Africa. Her narratives deal with men of British blood, plus Schwartz, whose work the Church of England adopted. She argues these laborers were practical and hard-working men. They were not the talking, unpractical men critics imagined. The book closes with lives reaching to Charles Mackenzie on the fever-haunted Zambesi.
poems-new-and-old:
John Freeman published Poems New and Old in London in 1920, with Selwyn and Blount, and the book opens with press notices praising his strange, desolate landscapes and beautiful rhythms. Critics quoted here call his nature poetry individual and slow to win readers, but lasting once won. The Times Literary Supplement praises the book as fragments of autobiography, the surrender of a man's inner life to the world.

An epigraph from an older poet sets the aim: to hear the music of the spheres and the angels singing. Freeman's poems pursue that rarefied air through English fields and skies, in verse the Westminster Gazette found aloof yet fascinating, reporting feelings not previously recorded in poetry. New and old work together let readers judge the claim: a quiet Georgian poet staking everything on the truth of a solitary, attentive spirit.
prose-idylls-new-and-old:
Charles Kingsley, clergyman and naturalist, collected essays on the English countryside in a new edition printed by Macmillan in 1882. Kingsley writes as a man who walked the fields and streams he describes and loved to teach others to look closely.

The six pieces are A Charm of Birds, Chalk-Stream Studies, The Fens, My Winter-Garden, From Ocean to Sea, and North Devon. Birds, fish, weather, and coast scenery fill the pages, mixed with moral reflection in his warm, urgent voice. Readers get Victorian nature writing that joins science, faith, and close watching of wild life.
queen-mary-and-harold: Queen Mary and Harold holds two dramas by Alfred, Lord Tennyson, Poet Laureate: Queen Mary and Harold. Only the contents and the cast list of the first play are shown. Queen Mary's people include the Queen herself and Philip of Spain. The Princess Elizabeth appears. Cardinal Pole appears too. So do the ambassadors Renard and Noailles. Archbishop Cranmer and Bishop Gardiner are listed. Edward Courtenay is there. Sir Thomas Wyatt stands among the rebel leaders.
raw-gold: Raw Gold, a novel by Bertrand W. Sinclair, illustrated by Clarence H. Rowe, was issued by G. W. Dillingham Company in June 1908, under copyrights of 1907 and 1908. The pages shown give the frontispiece. In it, Hicks draws on the narrator. His own finger curls on the trigger at the same moment. The first contents follow. The Long Arm of the Law opens the list. A Reminiscent Hour and Birds of Prey come next. A Tale Half Told, Mounted Again, and Stony Crossing follow. Thirty Days in Irons closes this part.
reginald:
Saki, the pen name of H. H. Munro, made his name with these sketches of Reginald, first printed in the Westminster Gazette. Methuen of London issued the third edition in 1911; the book first appeared in September 1904. Each piece puts Reginald in a fresh social scene and lets him talk.

Reginald holds forth on Christmas presents, on the Academy, and at the theatre. He offers a peace poem, joins a choir treat, and discourses on worries and house-parties. Further pieces place him at the Carlton, on besetting sins, and in a drama of his own. The sketches are short, polished, and dry, built on talk that sounds light and cuts deep.
round-the-world:
Andrew Carnegie wrote Round the World, a travel book first printed for private circulation, like his earlier An American Four-in-Hand in Britain. In the preface he says his publishers asked leave to give the book to the public. Kind reviews moved him less than letters from total strangers, still coming almost daily. Some came from invalids who thanked him for making their reading days pass more brightly. Carnegie calls those letters precious and makes their writers chiefly responsible for the volume.

Carnegie hopes readers will like the new book half as well as the first, though friends differ on which is better. While coaching, he says, he was more joyously happy. On the trip round the world he was gaining more knowledge. A short verse urges the traveler, on seeing some rare and noteworthy object, to think on friends and wish them sharers in the joy.
ruth-arnold: L. Byerley wrote Ruth Arnold, or The Country Cousin, issued in London by the Religious Tract Society. The contents list ten chapters, opening with A Letter, Talking It Over, Ruth's Decision, and The Journey. Later chapters are headed Cousins, Stonegate, A Poor Relation, Sea-side Pleasures, and The Picnic. The list closes with Busyborough as the tenth chapter. No preface or opening passage appears in the portion shown here.
sailing-alone-around-the-world: Captain Joshua Slocum wrote Sailing Alone Around the World, with pictures by Thomas Fogarty and George Varian. A photograph shows the Spray in Australian waters, and the book is given to the one who said the Spray will come back. The contents give full chapter outlines. Chapter I covers Slocum's blue-nose ancestry, his youthful fondness for the sea, his command of the Northern Light, the loss of the Aquidneck, and the rebuilding and launching of the Spray.
saturday-s-child:
Kathleen Norris's Saturday's Child appears as Volume IV of her works, under the nursery lines that Friday's child is loving and giving, but Saturday's child must work for her living. A dedication sonnet to C. G. N., signed from your wife, says the book has grown under both their hands. No living word of hers, she writes, could exist without the echo of his own. The days, talks, hopes, and fears that made the story are not hers to give, nor his alone. She offers his portion in grateful memory of four years.

Part One is headed Poverty. Chapter I opens in a dingy office on the mezzanine floor of a great wholesale drug house in San Francisco. The house is Hunter, Baxter and Hunter's, and the time is the beginning of the present century. Not the place, the narrator says, in which to look for the Great Adventure.
selections-from-the-prose-works-of-matth:
William Savage Johnson, professor of English at the University of Kansas, edited this college choice of Matthew Arnold's prose. Houghton Mifflin issued it in 1913 in the Riverside College Classics line, by leave of Arnold's American publishers. Johnson adds an opening essay and notes for students.

Arnold wrote on schools, faith, poetry, and the conduct of life with calm, high seriousness. Chosen essays let a class watch his mind at work across those fields. The volume served schools that wanted Arnold's criticism in one handy book, with help close at hand for young readers meeting his terms and allusions for the first time.
sienkiewicz-so-runs-the-world:
Shorter fiction by Sienkiewicz fills So Runs the World, here in English. Tales and sketches of modern Poland sit beside character studies and brief parables. The Nobel laureate works here on a smaller scale than in his vast historical epics.

Village folk, gentry, and dreamers pass through these pages in turn. Some tales cut with satire, while others rest in quiet pathos. His famed ease of telling never flags, even in a few pages. Readers who know Quo Vadis will find a fine companion here, proof that his range reached well beyond the epic canvas.
sir-francis-drake-s-famous-voyage-round-:
Francis Pretty, one of Drake's gentlemen at arms, told this tale of the famous voyage around the whole globe of the earth. The fleet set out from Plymouth on November 15, 1577: five ships and barks with 164 men, gentlemen and sailors. Its stated aim, Alexandria, hid the true design.

A tempest off Falmouth nearly wrecked the fleet at once. The Pelican, Drake's own ship, lost her mast overboard, while the Marigold drove ashore and took harm. Repairs at Plymouth sent them forth again on December 13. Pretty's plain record became a founding text of English sea adventure.
sketches-new-and-old:
Mark Twain gathered these sketches new and old into one full set, from My Watch and The Jumping Frog onward. Contents mix tales, speeches, and hoaxes: Journalism in Tennessee, the bad and good little boys, Niagara, and poultry raising all appear. The McWilliamses face membranous croup in one famed domestic piece.

Later pieces include the great beef contract, a medieval romance, a ghost story, and the Capitoline Venus. Speeches at a Scottish banquet in London and on accident insurance close the range. Twain's early newspaper humor stands complete here, wild, various, and already masterful.
social-life-in-the-insect-world: J. H. Fabre wrote Social Life in the Insect World, turned into English by Bernard Miall, with fourteen pictures. The London issue by T. Fisher Unwin lists a first edition of 1911 and ten more printings through 1918. The opening picture captions show the mantis: two females in a duel, and a mantis eating a cricket.
tales-for-young-and-old:
Tales for Young and Old opens with a short preface signed W. and R. C., explaining that the stories were written when the older among the intended readers were considerably younger and the young were in infancy. The contents list fourteen tales, from The Bride's Journey to The Locksmith of Philadelphia.

The first tale, The Bride's Journey by Mrs. Crowe, begins in 1809, when the French were in Prussia and M. Louison, an officer in the commissariat of the imperial army, fell in love with Adelaide Hext, the daughter of a respectable but not wealthy merchant. Her father detested the French, so the attachment, imprudently returned, starts under a ban. Love at first sight, a pledge redeemed, a blind man of Argenteuil, and a bridal wreath fill out the family anthology.
ten-days-that-shook-the-world:
John Reed wrote Ten Days That Shook the World as an eyewitness account of the Russian Revolution, in twelve chapters with notes and twelve appendices. Reed calls his book a slice of heightened history, history as he himself saw it.

He tells of the November Revolution, when the Bolsheviki led workers and soldiers to seize state power for the Soviets. Most scenes sit in Red Petrograd, the core of the revolt, though Reed notes the same acts played out across Russia. Readers get street-level scenes, speeches, and decrees from a reporter who stood inside the storm, still read as a key first-hand record of 1917.
the-admirable-tinker-child-of-the-world: Edgar Jepson wrote The Admirable Tinker, subtitled Child of the World, with art by Margaret Eckerson, printed in New York by McClure, Phillips and Co. in March 1904. Chapters listed run from Sir Tancred's Quest and The Finding of Tinker through The Training of Tinker, Tinker Intervenes, and Tinker Borrows a Motor-Car to Tinker Takes Septimus Rainer in Hand.
the-american-child: Front matter and contents open Elizabeth McCracken's The American Child, dated 1913, with pictures from photographs by Alice Austin. McCracken dedicates the book to her father and mother from Cambridge in January of that year. Six chapters follow a child through home, play, the country, school, the library, and church, ending with a closing section. The picture list names small girls, a boy of the house, a story hour in a children's room, and classes at school and in church.
the-appetite-of-tyranny-including-letter:
G. K. Chesterton groups four chapters and a set of letters in this wartime book. The chapters run from The Facts of the Case through The War on the Word and The Refusal of Reciprocity to the title piece and The Escape of Folly. Letters to an old Garibaldian follow.

Chesterton opens with a plain claim: behind even the most tangled business there is a story. A man who sets a house on fire may reveal the faults of its owners, drunk or stingy, but both still burned because he lit the fire. So too, he says, the facts of the present European blaze can be told plainly before deeper causes are weighed.
the-case-of-summerfield:
The Case of Summerfield, by William Henry Rhodes, is introduced by Geraldine Bonner as a tale rescued from oblivion. It first appeared in a San Francisco paper in 1871. It was signed only with the unknown name Caxton. At once the little world by the Golden Gate asked whether its contention could be true.

The contention was that, by the use of potassium, water could be set on fire, and that anyone holding that baneful secret could destroy the world. Told with bare directness, it sounded too real to be invention, and readers could not decide where truth and fiction blended. Bonner reveals Caxton as a lawyer of standing who drew the tale from his own studies in chemistry, which gave the story its convincing plausibility.
the-christmas-child: Hesba Stretton, author of Jessica's First Prayer, wrote this tale, published in New York by Thomas Y. Crowell and Company in September 1909, with pictures by K. Street. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here. The first chapters are titled The Coming of Joan, Joan's Search, and The Child in the Manger.A title page and a contents list are all that stand here.
the-clique-of-gold:
Emile Gaboriau opens this Paris novel at No. 23 in Grange Street, a house he calls the best kept and most inviting in the city. Neatness there is minute and extreme, with a touch of Holland about it. The brass plate on the door is polished bright enough for neighbors to shave in, and the stone floor shines.

Notices in the entrance hall, written in the style landlords love, ask tenants to respect the property of others. Clean your feet, they say, and no spitting on the stairs, and no dogs in the house. Yet for all its order, the house holds a sorry reputation in the neighborhood. Gaboriau wonders whether it is truly worse than No. 21 or No. 25, and answers probably not. Houses, like men, he argues, have their fates.
the-crock-of-gold: James Stephens wrote The Crock of Gold, printed with twelve color pictures by Thomas Mackenzie. Its contents divide the tale into six books: The Coming of Pan, The Philosopher's Journey, The Two Gods, The Philosopher's Return, The Policemen, and The Thin Woman's Journey and the Happy March. The frontispiece caption says the philosophers were able to hear each other thinking all day long. Only the title page, contents, and picture list are present here.
the-daemon-of-the-world:
Percy Bysshe Shelley calls The Daemon of the World a fragment. Part 1 opens under a Latin motto from Lucan's Pharsalia and turns at once to a question about death: How wonderful is Death, Death and his brother Sleep. One is pale as the wan, horned moon with lips of lurid blue; the other glows like the vital morning throned on ocean's wave.

The poem asks whether the iron-sceptred skeleton, whose reign lies in the tainted graves, has claimed a fair form whose azure veins steal like dark streams along a field of snow. Must that form decay and leave nothing but loathsomeness and ruin? Or do winged slumbers merely charm the sleeper, whose eyes will open with the morning beam? Ianthe, the poem says, does not sleep the dreamless sleep of death.
the-dweller-on-the-threshold:
Robert Hichens's novel The Dweller on the Threshold, dated 1911, opens with two men: Evelyn Malling, known for work in psychical research, and the Rev. Marcus Harding, a star London clergyman. Harding fills St. Joseph's, draws the largest Hospital Sunday gifts in town, and weds smart couples amid lilies and fine music. His wife, Lady Sophia, is able and admired.

Yet some flaw gnaws at Harding's gift, and Malling watches it grow. Hichens, who wrote The Garden of Allah, blends church success with occult dread. A man's double and his soul's price drive the tale.
the-education-of-the-child:
Ellen Key's The Education of the Child opens with praise from Edward Bok of the Ladies' Home Journal, who calls it a classic that should sit in every home with a child. Key builds on Goethe's Werther: the child's will holds the seed of future strength, and each fault hides a germ of good. Force a child to your own shape, she warns, and you break that germ.

Children, she holds, must not be treated as subjects with no will of their own. Key's book helped launch a century that put the child's nature first in schools and homes.
the-english-orphans-or-a-home-in-the-new:
Mrs. Mary J. Holmes's The English Orphans; or, A Home in the New World is dated 1877 in its front pages. Contents open with The Emigrants and Chicopee, then Billy Bender, Ella Campbell, and The Poor-House. Winter at the poor-house, a new bonnet, and a new home in Rice Corner chart the girls' slow climb.

Orphan sisters cross the sea and face want in Massachusetts. Holmes, famed for Lena Rivers and Tempest and Sunshine, wrote for a vast home readership. Tears, grit, and kind friends carry her heroines from the poor-house to love and place.
the-eyes-of-the-world:
Harold Bell Wright set his novel The Eyes of the World at Tecolote Rancho, and the dedication is dated April 13, 1914. He gives the book to Benjamin H. Pearson, a friend from the Pipe-Line Trail camp in the San Bernardino hills.

Before the story starts, Wright prints lines from Wordsworth on looking at nature with a graver, sadder sense. The quote speaks of a presence felt in sunsets, ocean, air, and sky, and in the mind of man. That mood frames a tale where the high peaks and quiet camps of the West shape how its people see their lives.
the-furnace-of-gold: Philip Verrill Mighels wrote The Furnace of Gold as a western novel of the Nevada gold camps, under copyrights of 1909 and 1910. Only the front matter and part of the contents are present here. The heads name a prince or bandit, a trip into the mountains, a rescue, a battle, the Laughing Water claim, and a man named Bostwick losing ground. Mighels' past books named here include The Pillars of Eden and Bruvver Jim's Baby. No chapter text can be read here.
the-golden-threshold: Sarojini Naidu wrote The Golden Threshold. It is a book of poems. Arthur Symons wrote the introduction. Naidu dedicated it to Edmund Gosse. Gosse first showed her the way to the golden threshold. The title page notes London, 1896, and Hyderabad, 1905. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list in three groups. Folk Songs name Palanquin-Bearers, Indian Weavers, and Coromandel Fishers. Poems name an ode to the Nizam of Hyderabad and Indian Dancers.
the-home-and-the-world:
Rabindranath Tagore wrote The Home and the World. The pages present date Tagore 1861-1941. Surendranath Tagore translated the book from Bengali to English. Macmillan published it in London in 1919. Indian publication came in 1915 and 1916. Chapter one is Bimala's story. Bimala recalls her mother with love.

Her mother wore a vermilion mark at the parting of her hair. Her sari had a wide red border. Her eyes were full of depth and peace. Everyone said Bimala resembled her mother. In childhood Bimala resented the mirror for that likeness. She thought her dark features an unfairness from God. She asked only to grow into a model of womanhood.
the-iron-rule-or-tyranny-in-the-househol:
T. S. Arthur, the Philadelphia temperance novelist, published this tale of tyranny in the household in 1853. Chapter I introduces Andrew Howland, one of those rigid moralists who can tolerate no wanderings from the right way in others. His children were straitjacketed into outward consistency from infancy. Punishment surely followed any step off the line they were required to walk.

Arthur complicates the portrait at once: a child loves his parent naturally, and golden threads of love mingle with fear in the Howland children. Their mother grew up in a home where children's laughter was rarely checked, and checked without wounding, before she was transplanted into this sterner household. The novel sets gentle upbringing against the iron rule to show what domestic tyranny does to a family from inside.
the-ivory-child:
H. Rider Haggard returns to Allan Quatermain here. The contents promise a shooting lesson and a bet. A bona fide gold mine follows. Lord Ragnall tells his story. A desert meeting, a capture, and an elephant named Jana come next. A chase, a cave dweller, and a sanctuary oath close the list. Quatermain calls it perhaps his strangest adventure. His whole life can scarcely be called tame or humdrum.

He previews the puzzle himself. War comes against the Black Kendah people. Jana, their elephant god, will die. Quatermain wondered whether the beast was more than a gigantic animal. The White Kendah's magic gets a skeptic's footnote. Harût and Marût divined that he alone could kill Jana. They invited him for that purpose. Hans killed the elephant in the end. Jana nearly killed Quatermain first.
the-junior-classics-volume-5-stories-tha: Volume five of The Junior Classics is titled Stories That Never Grow Old. William Patten selected the set for boys and girls. Charles W. Eliot wrote its introduction. William Allan Neilson supplied a reading guide. A Rackham picture fronts this volume. Only the title pages and contents start are present here. The stories themselves do not appear. The contents begin with the Arabian Nights. Ali Baba, Aladdin, and Sindbad the Sailor appear. Robinson Crusoe follows, shipwrecked and alone. Daniel Defoe is credited for Crusoe's chapters.
the-life-and-death-of-cormac-the-skald:
An unknown Icelandic writer composed the saga of Cormac the skald sometime between 1250 and 1300, perhaps from a lost twelfth century tale. W. G. Collingwood and J. Stefansson translated it in 1901. Chapter one begins in the days of King Harald Fairhair of Norway.

A champion named Cormac serves the king, and his son Ogmund grows big and sturdy, roving at sea each summer. Ogmund fights the champion Asmund Ashenside for four days around the British Isles and wins wealth and honor. A marriage to Helga, daughter of Earl Frodi, follows, setting up the poet hero line.
the-lure-of-the-labrador-wild:
Dillon Wallace wrote The Lure of the Labrador Wild, the story of the exploring expedition conducted by Leonidas Hubbard, Jr. In a preface to the sixth edition, Wallace says three years have passed since Hubbard and he began that fateful journey. A little more than a year has passed since the first edition appeared. He has since looked behind the ranges himself, returning over Grand Lake into the wilderness that lured Hubbard to his death. Wallace relives the fatal choice in detail.

In June of the previous year he stood again where they passed by the bay receiving the Nascaupee River, the trail they were searching for. Hubbard, resting on his paddle, had called it just a bay not worth exploring. A perceptible current, a questioning word, or a turn of a paddle would have set them right.
the-master-of-the-world:
Jules Verne's The Master of the World is narrated by a head inspector in the federal police department at Washington. He warns readers that the events rank among the most extraordinary the twentieth century will witness. Strange happenings in the mountains open the case, around a peak called the Great Eyrie. The contents follow mysterious machines seen along the New England shores and at Niagara.

Letters arrive from an unknown inventor who places himself outside the law. A campaign against his machine ends aboard a vessel called the Terror. Late chapters name Robur, the Conqueror, tying the mystery to Verne's earlier airship captain. The inspector admits that some facts rest on his word alone. Readers get a chase after a machine that masters land, sea, and air, told by the man assigned to catch it.
the-moving-picture-girls-under-the-palms:
Laura Lee Hope's The Moving Picture Girls Under the Palms carries the subtitle Lost in the Wilds of Florida. Only title page and the first lines of a contents list are present here. The Florida story itself does not appear. Grosset and Dunlap held the copyright in 1914, and the World Syndicate Publishing Company published the volume at Cleveland and New York.

Just four chapters are listed. Overboard opens the book at page 1, and To the Rescue follows at page 11. A Disquieting Item at page 18 and Fire on Board at page 28 complete what is shown. Hope is billed on the title page as author of the Moving Picture Girls at Oak Farm, the Bobbsey Twins series, and the Outdoor Girls series.
the-nervous-child:
Hector Charles Cameron's The Nervous Child is present here only in title pages and a partial contents list, so the medical guidance itself does not appear. Cameron, a physician at Guy's Hospital in London in charge of its children's department, is named with his Cambridge and London degrees. An Emerson saying heads the title page: respect the child, and do not trespass on his solitude.

The printing history on the page is double: a first edition of 1919 and a second impression dated 1930 are both stated. Contents shown run to six chapters, from Doctors, Mothers, and Children through nursery observations and want of appetite, to want of sleep, other signs of nervousness, and enuresis, or bed-wetting.
the-palmy-days-of-nance-oldfield: Edward Robins wrote The Palmy Days of Nance Oldfield, published in 1898 with portraits. Only the front matter, contents, and portrait list are present here, so the biography itself does not appear. The contents trace the actress Anne Oldfield from tavern to theatre, through chapters on managerial wickedness, tragic paths, and the fading of a star. Portraits include Oldfield as Fair Rosamond, Colley Cibber, Robert Wilks, William Congreve, and Joseph Addison.
the-religious-life-of-the-zun-i-child:
Mrs. Tilly E. Stevenson reports on Zuni childhood religion. She writes for the Smithsonian Institution's Bureau of Ethnology. Contents list a brief account of Zuni mythology first. Birth customs follow in the list. Two forms of initiation come next. One form is involuntary, and one is voluntary. Both lead into the Kok-ko society. Page numbers run into the five hundreds.

Plates show Zuni masks and groups of masked figures. A sand altar in the kiva of the North appears. The kiva of the East appears as well. Only the title page is present here. The contents and illustration list appear with it. Stevenson's account itself does not appear on these pages.
the-rivals-of-acadia-an-old-story-of-the: An old story of the New World was entered for copyright at Boston on January 26, 1827, by publishers Wells and Lilly, who claimed the right as proprietors. A Shakespeare motto warns that when two authorities stand with neither supreme, confusion soon enters between them. Here only the title page and the copyright entry are present, and no author is named on these pages, so the Acadian rivalry itself does not appear.
the-shield: A volume titled The Shield is represented here by a publisher's list and a transcriber's note. No author is named in the pages shown. The list advertises the newest Borzoi books. Central Europe by Friedrich Naumann and Crimes of Charity by Konrad Bercovici appear. The Journal of Leo Tolstoi is also listed. The transcriber's note says inconsistent hyphenation and unusual spelling were preserved. Obvious typographical errors were corrected, it adds. No title page beyond the book's name, no contents, and no chapter text are present.
the-soul-of-a-child:
Edwin Björkman published this novel in 1922, arranging a boy's growing awareness in four parts. The story belongs to Keith, whose earliest consciousness of himself and the world forms in a three-room flat on the fourth floor of a house in old Stockholm.

Björkman first maps that setting in loving detail. The rocky island was once the whole city. It holds the Royal Palace, Great Square with its Christmas toy market, and narrow lanes running down to the waterfronts. Keith's parents live above dingy shops in a lane near the palace, among humble middle-class families crowded into gloomy old apartments, and the city itself shapes the child's inner life.
the-story-of-a-child:
Pierre Loti's autobiographical account of his childhood appears in Caroline F. Smith's translation, introduced by a long preface on the modern movement to study child life. The preface grants that child study is not new, since every wise parent and sympathetic teacher has always practised it, but notes a new effort to pursue it consciously and systematically.

Early hopes that the new psychology would revolutionize education have met reaction, the preface admits, because education can never be reduced to mere science and must rely on instinct, tact, and appreciation. Against that background Loti's intimate record of one child's inner world is offered as the human evidence that theory cannot supply.
the-top-of-the-world: Ethel M. Dell's Top of the World, dated 1920, is shown here through its dedication leaves and the start of a contents list. Dell dedicates the novel to her mother's memory, under a poem asking how a climber reaches the top of the world. The poem answers that wealth, success, and fame will pall; the goal is reached by faith and love. The contents then open Part One and stop. Dell's romance itself does not begin in the pages present, though its moral compass is plain.
the-two-guardians-or-home-in-this-world:
Charlotte Mary Yonge's Two Guardians, or Home in This World, in its 1871 printing, opens with her preface on the design of her tales. She says the moral has been thought not evident enough, because she preferred suggestion to direct preaching. Throughout her stories the plan is to picture ordinary life, its small daily events, pleasures, and trials, turned to the best account. Great events are excluded, exciting incidents sacrificed, and interest made to depend on character painting.

Each tale illustrates a key-note principle. Abbeychurch shows self-control's necessity, and the harm conceit does. Scenes and Characters contrasts guidance by mere feeling against strict adherence to duty. Henrietta's Wish opposes wilfulness to submission. Yonge's preface is a small manifesto for the domestic novel of conscience, explaining how quiet lives are meant to carry moral weight.
the-two-sides-of-the-shield:
Charlotte M. Yonge returns in a preface to people she created years earlier in Scenes and Characters, her second book. Readers had written asking what became of favourite figures, so she sets out their later careers here. She also promises that newcomers can follow the new story without knowing the older one.

At its centre stands the motherless Mohun family of Beechcroft, headed by a kindly deaf father nicknamed the Baron. The preface recalls a household thrown into confusion when an indolent sister took charge, romantic notions replaced duty, and younger boys fell into mischief. Marriage brought order before, and the novel follows what time has done to that family since.
the-untilled-field:
George Moore collects Irish stories in The Untilled Field, and the first, In the Clay, opens on a fine summer morning. Rodney, a sculptor, returns from his walk to the mews where his studio stands. His charwoman waits oddly in the middle of the roadway, and both studio doors stand wide open.

Rodney instantly fears for his just-finished Virgin and Child, the one piece he values among busts and replaceable sketches. The woman reports a night break-in, a hasp forced, and some things broken. Contents pages list thirteen stories in all, including The Exile, Home Sickness, A Letter to Rome, Julia Cahill's Curse, The Wedding-Gown, and The Wild Goose.
the-vicar-of-wakefield: Oliver Goldsmith presents The Vicar of Wakefield as a tale supposed to be written by the vicar himself, under a Latin motto hoping for the wretched and warning the fortunate. The material present here is the title page and a bare chapter list, so the story itself does not appear. Thirty-two chapters are numbered without titles, followed by an advertisement heading whose text is not included. Readers can confirm the book's identity and its length in chapters, nothing of Dr. Primrose's story.
the-way-of-the-wild: F. St. Mars wrote The Way of the Wild as a book of animal stories, with illustrations from photographs. The pages present here give the title page and contents, so the stories themselves do not appear. Ten chapters take a creature each: the way of the wolf, the rat, the weasel, the stoat, the sheep, the dog, and the bee. A chapter on how to tame a wild whelp closes the collection. Frontispieces show a grey wolf and Saro the Guiana potto, and plates include Red Slayer the weasel.
the-way-of-the-world:
William Congreve's Way of the World is taken here from Methuen's 1895 edition of his comedies, second volume. A dedication letter to Ralph, Earl of Mountague, precedes the play. Congreve admits uncertainty over whether dedicating the comedy looks like vanity, then argues that his lordship's patronage will supply whatever value the play lacks while it remains his.

He confesses the stage success surprised him, since little in the piece suits the audience's predominant taste. Gross fools, he says, deserve compassion more than laughter. His design instead makes characters ridiculous through affected, false wit rather than natural folly, which cannot be corrected. Hasty critics, he complains, fired their censure for two or three days before understanding their aim.
the-wedge-of-gold: C. C. Goodwin's Wedge of Gold carries a preface signed at Salt Lake City in June 1896, in which he recalls seeing the world's greatest gold mine. Only that preface and a chapter list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. Goodwin says his story is fictitious but built on true incidents, including the 1849 migration and the fortunes won and lost in mining camps. He promises pleasure, profit, sadness, biography, and history from it. Chapters close with an author's farewell.
the-wide-wide-world: Elizabeth Wetherell is named as editor of the very first edition of The Wide, Wide World. The present text comes from a 1902 edition prepared by the Reverend Allan Pollok, issued by the Religious Tract Society in London. The society issued this edition to mark the book's fiftieth anniversary. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. Contents promise a preface to the fiftieth anniversary edition, then forty-eight chapters. The first is named Mother and Child.
the-winds-of-the-world:
Talbot Mundy's Winds of the World carries a 1915 date in its heading and opens with a poem called Yasmini's Song. The verses send the winds of the world faring east, west, south, and north like shuttles weaving, and they counsel wise men to hearken when tracks cross and scent goes stale. Fools shout, the song says, and the fast fail.

Chapter one sets a rainy July field-day in the Punjab. A watery sun hurries down while native Indian cavalry gleams motionless between British infantry and horse artillery. A general explains and asserts pride in his command but never mentions why the exercises run in mud, why censorship is in full force, or anything of Germany or Belgium. War hangs unspoken over the parade.
the-wood-beyond-the-world:
William Morris wrote this tale of a quest in a made up world in 1894. Many call it the first modern fantasy set in a world made whole from the mind. Morris had made his own line of prose romance, in a high style of his own.

Golden Walter flees a bad marriage by sea and is cast on a strange shore past the world's rim. A wood of wonders, a cruel maid, and a kind one mark his road home and to love. The book founds the line of tales set in a second world, made new from whole cloth.
the-young-man-and-the-world: Albert J. Beveridge's The Young Man and the World, published by Appleton in 1905, is shown through its contents list. Eleven chapters guide a young man from his old home to a new one. College gets a chapter, split for those who go and those who cannot. The young lawyer's beginnings and public speaking follow. The pulpit and the nation also receive chapters. The essays themselves do not appear in the pages present in this record.
this-simian-world:
Clarence Day Jr. opens with a quotation from W. N. P. Barbellion, who proudly claimed kinship with other animals and a simian ancestry. Day then rides with Potter along upper Broadway on a mild Sunday afternoon. Crowds stroll, stare, and talk without going anywhere.

Potter despairs at their aimless mass and asks whether any creature besides vermin gathers so. Day answers that theirs is a simian civilization, run by ape descendants. Readers get a humorous essay in book form, using animal comparison to judge human crowds, cities, and habits with affectionate scepticism.
to-have-and-to-hold: Mary Johnston dedicated her novel to her mother's memory, and its contents run to thirty-seven chapters told in the first person. Headings announce throwing ambs-ace, meeting Master Jeremy Sparrow, marrying in haste, and repenting at leisure. A woman has her way, and the company goes to Jamestown. Later headings promise fighting Spaniards, a haunted wood, a grave dug, a trial, and guests of an emperor. A chapter list alone is present here, so Johnston's Virginia romance itself is not shown.
un-doc-declaration-of-the-rights-of-the-:
The Declaration of the Rights of the Child was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly on 20 November 1959. It builds on a 1924 Geneva text of the same name. Children need special care before and after birth, the preamble says. Mankind owes the child the best it has to give.

Ten short principles carry the message. Each child holds every right here, with no bar of birth or creed. The child's best interests rule when laws are made. A child gets a name and a nationality from birth. Food, housing, health care, and free basic schooling are all promised. So are play, love, and first call on relief. No child may be trafficked, neglected, or put to harmful work.
what-s-wrong-with-the-world: Here readers meet only the title page and a long contents list for G. K. Chesterton's What's Wrong with the World, so his essays do not appear. The list divides the book into four parts on man, empire, woman, and the child. Part one treats the homelessness of man and foes of property. Part three takes up votes for women and the modern slave. Part four turns to schools and the tricks of environment. The chapter names alone show Chesterton's love of paradox.
with-botha-in-the-field: The front pages here give the title page and the start of a contents list for Moore Ritchie's With Botha in the Field, printed in 1915, with no narrative present. Ritchie drew most of the book's eighty-two pictures himself, and five diagrams aid the text. A photo shows Generals Botha and Smuts meeting in the field before Windhuk was taken. The contents begin with part one, named Chasing the Rebels. A short dedication in French and English recalls shared days.
